subject: rla
title: The Extended Response I: Evaluating Two Arguments, Planning, and Writing a Thesis
objectives: You will explain what the GED Extended Response asks and how it is scored on three traits (argument and evidence; development and organization; clarity and conventions), each worth 0 to 2 points.
You will evaluate the evidence in two opposing argument passages with five questions: source, specific, relevant, sufficient, and fair, and name faulty reasoning.
You will decide which of two positions is better supported, based on evidence rather than personal opinion.
You will write a thesis that names the better-supported side, gives evidence-based reasons, and mentions both authors.
You will plan a response with a two-column organizer and build body paragraphs with Point, Evidence, Explain, Link.

slides.title: The Extended Response I: Evaluating Two Arguments, Planning, and Writing a Thesis
slides.board:
Week 9 · Reasoning Through Language Arts

Today you will:

  • Learn what the Extended Response asks and how the 3 traits are scored
  • Test evidence with five questions and spot faulty reasoning
  • Decide which of two arguments is better supported
  • Write a thesis that names a side, gives reasons, and mentions both authors
  • Plan in 10 minutes and build body paragraphs with P-E-E-L

Plan: Warm-up · Task and rubric · Evidence · Verdict · Thesis · Plan · Model response · Your turn · GED questions · Recap

notes.say:
Welcome to week 9. Today we start the Extended Response, the 45-minute essay on the RLA test. Many students fear it more than any other part of the GED, but it rewards a method more than talent, and you already own most of the tools: claims and evidence from week 5, comparing two texts from week 6, and the grammar from weeks 7 and 8. Today is about the thinking before the writing: judging two arguments, choosing the better-supported one, writing a thesis, and planning. Next week we organize, revise, and edit a full draft.

Before we start, open the Student Lesson in a second tab. The two ballpark passages we use all hour are on screens 7 and 8.
ask: Have you ever written a timed essay? What was the hardest part? (expected: any honest answer; listen for “I didn't know what to write first” or “I ran out of time,” and promise a plan for both)

slides.title: Warm-up: Grammar II review
slides.board:
Fix each sentence. Say the rule.

  1. Each of the authors (use / uses) evidence from a study.
  2. Osei's figures are clearer (then / than) Bell's.
  3. The team's study had a strong (affect / effect) on the council.
  4. bell's argument depends on it's own study.

These are the same skills scorers check in Trait 3 of your essay.
steps: 1. uses. The subject is “Each,” which is singular; “of the authors” is a phrase in the middle.
2. than. Use than to compare; then is about time.
3. effect. After “a strong,” you need a noun, a result. Affect is usually the verb.
4. Bell's argument depends on its own study. Capitalize the name; its (belongs to) has no apostrophe; it's means “it is.”

notes.say: This warm-up reviews last week: agreement, confused words, capitals, and apostrophes. I am framing it as Trait 3 on purpose. On the Extended Response, there is no spell-check and no grammar check, so these are the errors scorers will see in your essay. Give the student about 30 seconds per sentence and ask for the rule, not just the answer.
ask: In sentence 1, what is the subject? (expected: Each)
How can you test it's vs. its? (expected: read it as “it is”; if that makes no sense, use its)
notes.answer: 1. uses (singular subject “Each”). 2. than (comparison). 3. effect (noun, a result). 4. Bell's argument depends on its own study. (capital B; its with no apostrophe)
notes.watch: Sentence 4 has two errors. If the student fixes only one, say “There is one more” and wait. On the essay, students often fix the first error they see and stop looking.

slides.title: The task: be the judge, not a player
slides.board:
“In your response, analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from both articles to support your response.”

The question is NOTThe question IS
Which side do you agree with?Which author proved their side better?
  • 45 minutes · typed · two passages on opposite sides
  • Evidence from both passages
  • No spell-check

notes.say: Read the prompt slowly and stop on each underlined phrase. Analyze both positions means you discuss both authors. Which one is best supported means you are a judge weighing proof, not a voter sharing an opinion. Evidence from both articles means one passage is not enough: you show the strengths of one and the weaknesses of the other. A student can personally disagree with the better-supported side and still earn a top score. Usually one passage is clearly stronger, and choosing it makes the essay much easier to write.
ask: If you love baseball, do you have to argue for the ballpark? (expected: no; you argue for whichever author proved their case better)
What three phrases in the prompt tell you what to do? (expected: analyze both positions; which one is best supported; evidence from both articles)
notes.watch: The most common failure is writing “I believe the city should…” If you hear that, ask, “Who proved it better, Bell or Osei?”

slides.title: How the essay is scored: 3 traits, 0–2 each
slides.board:
TraitScorers look for
1. Argument and evidenceA clear position on which side is better supported; specific evidence from both passages; why it is strong or weak
2. Development and organizationIntroduction, body, conclusion; ideas that build logically; transitions; precise words; formal style and tone
3. Clarity and conventionsSentence structure: clear, varied, no run-ons or fragments; standard grammar, usage, capitalization, punctuation

Each trait: 2 = strong · 1 = partly there · 0 = missing

Trait points (0–6) are doubled: up to 12 raw points of your RLA score.

notes.say: Each trait is scored 0, 1, or 2, so an essay earns 0 to 6 trait points. The GED then doubles that raw score, so the essay is worth up to 12 raw points on the RLA test, roughly a fifth of the test's raw points. That is why it is worth real practice. Trait 1 is about thinking: did you pick a side and prove it with the passages? Trait 2 is about shape and style: can a reader follow your essay from the introduction to the conclusion, with clear transitions, precise words, and a formal tone? Trait 3 is about sentences: are they complete, varied, and correct, so a reader can understand every one? Scorers know this is a 45-minute first draft, so a few small errors are fine; errors that block meaning are not. An essay that is off topic, copies the passages, or is blank can get no credit at all.
ask: An essay is beautifully written but never mentions either passage. Which trait suffers most? (expected: Trait 1)
What is the highest total of trait points? (expected: 6, because 3 traits × 2 points)
If an essay earns 2, 1, and 2 on the three traits, how many raw points does it add to the RLA score? (expected: 5 trait points, doubled to 10)
notes.watch: Students think good grammar can save a weak argument. It cannot: grammar lives in Trait 3 only. Trait 1 needs evidence from both passages and an explanation of why it matters.

slides.title: Score it by trait
slides.board:
A student wrote this about the ballpark passages:

Ballparks are great for cities. I went to a game in Harlan City once, and downtown was really busy. Everyone loves baseball, so Port Delaney should build the ballpark. It would be fun for families.

Which trait needs the most work, and why?
steps: Trait 3: sentences are clear and correct. Not the main problem.
Trait 2: very thin, but there is a point and a reason. Weak, not the biggest issue.
Trait 1: argues the writer's own view (“should build”), uses the writer's own trip, and never names Bell or Osei or uses their evidence.
Verdict: Trait 1 needs the most work. Fix: judge which author is better supported, with evidence from both passages.

notes.say: Model how a scorer reads: check each trait in turn and look for proof, not effort. This paragraph is clear and nearly error-free, so a student might think it scores well. Walk through the three traits and show that the real problem is Trait 1: it argues the student's own opinion and never uses Bell or Osei.
ask: What would the first sentence of a better paragraph look like? (expected: something like “Bell's evidence for the ballpark is weaker than it looks.”)

slides.title: Test the evidence: five questions
slides.board:
1. Source: Who says so? Expert? Named? Gains from the result?
  2. Specific: Numbers, dates, named studies, or vague words?
  3. Relevant: Does it prove this claim?
  4. Sufficient: Enough? One story is not a pattern.
  5. Fair: Does the author deal honestly with the other side?

Red flags

  • Hasty generalization: one case → a rule
  • Bandwagon: “everyone agrees”
  • Slippery slope: one step → disaster
  • Emotional appeal in place of proof
  • Unsupported claim: no source at all

notes.say: These five questions are the heart of the lesson. Week 5 gave us claims, evidence, and faulty reasoning; now we use them as a judge. Ask all five of every important piece of evidence. Stress two ideas. First, specific is not the same as reliable: a number from a source that profits from the result can still be weak. Second, a fair author who admits the other side's good points usually becomes more believable, not less.
ask: A gym says, “82 percent of our members plan to renew,” from its own survey. Which question raises a concern? (expected: Source; the gym gains from good results)
Your neighbor says the gym is the best in town. Which questions does that fail? (expected: Specific and Sufficient; it is one opinion with no numbers)
notes.watch: Students tend to grade evidence by how impressive it sounds. Make them name the question it passes or fails every time.

slides.title: Test one piece of evidence
slides.board:
Bell, paragraph 2:

“A study commissioned by the Pelicans found that the new ballpark would create 1,200 jobs and bring $30 million a year into the local economy.”

Strong or weak? Run the five questions.
steps: Source: the Pelicans paid for the study, and the Pelicans get the ballpark. The source gains from the result.
Specific: yes, 1,200 jobs and $30 million. It sounds strong.
Relevant: yes, it speaks to jobs and spending.
Check the other passage: Osei (para. 3) says the team plays about 70 home games a year, most ballpark jobs are part-time and seasonal, and the study never says how many jobs are full-time.
Verdict: weak. Specific is not the same as reliable.

notes.say: Show the student how to run the test out loud. The number sounds impressive, which is exactly why this example matters. Then go to the other passage: a strong essay uses Passage B to show what Passage A's numbers leave out. Teach the phrase “specific is not the same as reliable.”
ask: Who paid for the study? (expected: the Pelicans, the team that wants the ballpark)

slides.title: Name the faulty reasoning
slides.board:
Bell writes:

  1. “My brother-in-law lives in Harlan City… He says downtown Harlan City is now packed… If it worked for Harlan City, it will work for us.”
  2. “Everyone I talk to downtown is excited.”
  3. “The ballpark will pay for itself many times over.”

Name the flaw in each.
steps: 1. Hasty generalization (an anecdote): one relative's impression of one city becomes a rule for Port Delaney. Fails Sufficient, and it never proves the stadium caused the change.
2. Bandwagon: popularity is not proof, and “everyone I talk to” is a small, unnamed group. Fails Source and Specific.
3. Unsupported claim: no figures at all. Fails Specific. Osei's numbers (repay $77.5 million, collect $400,000 a year) point the other way.

notes.say: Each of these sentences feels persuasive, and each fails a test. Name the flaw, then say which of the five questions it fails. Naming the flaw gives the student precise words for the essay: “Bell relies on a hasty generalization” earns more than “Bell is wrong.”
ask: Which of the three would you attack first in your essay, and why? (expected: any with a reason; the Harlan City story is a good choice because Bell treats it as proof)
notes.watch: If the student says the Harlan City story is “a fact,” ask, “Who measured it?” It is a relative's impression, not a measurement.

slides.title: Together: judge a mini-pair
slides.board:
Writer 1: Ashford should add a 10-cent deposit on bottles and cans. When neighboring Glen Ridge County added the same deposit in 2019, its public works department counted 58 percent fewer bottles and cans along county roadsides by 2022. Stores did need space for return machines, so Glen Ridge let small shops send returns to a central recycling center instead.

Writer 2: A bottle deposit is just another tax on working families. Everyone knows people will throw their bottles away anyway. Store owners I've met hate the idea. If we start charging deposits on bottles, soon there will be a fee on everything we buy.

(a) Each claim? (b) Strongest evidence? (c) Two flaws in Writer 2? (d) How does Writer 1 treat the other side?
steps: (a) Writer 1: Ashford should add a 10-cent deposit. Writer 2: Ashford should not.
(b) The Glen Ridge public works count: 58 percent fewer bottles and cans by 2022. Named source, specific, relevant.

(c) Any two: “Everyone knows” (bandwagon, no proof) · “Store owners I've met” (vague, unnamed) · “soon there will be a fee on everything” (slippery slope) · calling a refundable deposit a “tax” without explaining.
(d) Writer 1 admits stores need space and explains Glen Ridge's fix. Dealing fairly with a problem makes the argument more credible.

notes.say: The student leads; you guide. Read both writers aloud, then take the questions one at a time. Reveal each step only after the student answers. Point out how short Writer 1 is: one strong, specific, sourced fact can outweigh a paragraph of opinions.
ask: Is a deposit really a tax? What does the passage suggest? (expected: no; you get the deposit back when you return the bottle, and Writer 2 never addresses that)
notes.answer: (a) Writer 1: add the deposit; Writer 2: do not. (b) The Glen Ridge count of 58 percent fewer bottles and cans by 2022. (c) Any two of: bandwagon (“Everyone knows”), vague source (“Store owners I've met”), slippery slope (“a fee on everything”), unexplained label (“tax”). (d) It admits the space problem and gives Glen Ridge's solution.
notes.watch: Students sometimes pick “Store owners I've met hate the idea” as strong evidence because store owners are affected. Ask: how many owners, which ones, and how would we check?

slides.title: Which side is better supported? The scorecard
slides.board:
For each passage, ask
1. Best evidenceDoes it survive the five questions?
2. Weakest evidenceBiased, vague, one story, or no source?
3. Red flagsHow many, and how central to the argument?
4. The other sideAnswered fairly, ignored, or mocked?

Better supported = the side whose key evidence survives testing and who deals fairly with the other side.

Not: longer · more emotional · more confident · the side you agree with

notes.say: Now we go from single pieces of evidence to a verdict. Fill in the scorecard for both passages, then compare. The stronger side does not need to be perfect; it needs better proof for its main claims. Warn the student about the traps: length, emotion, confidence, and personal agreement do not decide the winner. Also, do not assume the side arguing “no” always wins. In this week's practice, the side arguing “yes” is better supported in one pair.
ask: Can the better-supported side have a flaw? (expected: yes; it only needs stronger support overall, and admitting its flaw is part of a fair essay)
notes.watch: Some students count facts: “Osei has more numbers, so she wins.” Push for quality: which numbers come from reliable sources and actually prove the claim?

slides.title: The verdict: Bell vs. Osei
slides.board:
Bell (build it)Osei (do not)
Best evidenceTeam-paid study: 1,200 jobs30+ years of independent studies; $77.5M repaid vs. $400K a year rent
Red flagsAnecdote, bandwagon, “pays for itself”Few; does not name the studies
Other sideWaves off cost criticsAdmits fans would be sad; offers a middle path

Who is better supported?
steps: Best evidence: Osei's is independent and checkable; Bell's comes from a source that gains from the result.
Red flags: Bell's argument leans on three; Osei's has one small gap.
Other side: Osei answers Bell's best point (the team could leave); Bell brushes off cost.
Verdict: Osei is better supported, by evidence, not by opinion about baseball.

notes.say: Walk through each row and compare. Point out that Osei is not perfect: she describes the studies but does not name them. A fair essay can admit that. Still, her best evidence survives the five questions and Bell's does not. Notice we do the math check too: $3.1 million times 25 years is $77.5 million.
ask: What is Bell's single best point? (expected: the lease ends in two years and the owners may look at other cities)

slides.title: The thesis: one sentence, three jobs
slides.board:
1. Name the side that is better supported
  2. Give the reasons (evidence-based)
  3. Mention both authors

Frame: ___'s argument is better supported because ___, while ___ relies on ___.

Where: the last sentence of your introduction. It is also your outline.

notes.say: A thesis is the one sentence your whole essay proves. On this essay it has three jobs: name the side, give the reasons, and mention both authors. The frame does all three. Show the student that the thesis is also the plan: the “because” part becomes the body paragraph on the stronger side, and the “while … relies on” part becomes the body paragraph on the weaker side.
ask: Why put the “while” clause in the thesis? (expected: it mentions the other author and sets up the paragraph about the weaker side's evidence)
notes.watch: Students write “I think” or “I believe” in the thesis. It is not wrong grammar, but it pulls them toward opinion. Teach “___'s argument is better supported because…” instead.

slides.title: The thesis ladder
slides.board:
1. “I think a ballpark is a waste of money.”
  2. “Both authors make good points.”
  3. “Osei's argument is better supported.”
  4. “Osei's argument is better supported because she relies on independent research and specific cost figures, while Bell relies on a team-funded study, one personal story, and appeals to pride.”

Climb the ladder: what does each rung lack?
steps: Rung 1: personal opinion; does not mention either passage.
Rung 2: no position. Fairness belongs in the body, but the thesis must choose.
Rung 3: takes a side, but no reasons and only one author.
Rung 4: all three jobs. It is also the outline for the body paragraphs.

notes.say: Read each rung and ask which of the three jobs it does. Each rung fixes one problem of the one before it. Only the top rung names a side, gives evidence-based reasons, and mentions both authors.
ask: Rung 4 names three of Bell's weaknesses. Where will each one go in the essay? (expected: in the body paragraph about Bell's evidence)

slides.title: Together: fix the thesis
slides.board:
Bottle-deposit pair. Fix each thesis.

  1. “Bottle deposits are a good idea because I hate seeing trash on the road.”
  2. “Writer 2 makes some good points, but so does Writer 1.”
  3. “Writer 1 is better.”

Then write one strong thesis with the frame.
steps: 1. Personal opinion. Fix: judge the writers, not the deposit.
2. No position. Fix: choose the side with stronger evidence.
3. No reasons, one author. Fix: add “because…” and “while Writer 2…”

Sample: “Writer 1's argument is better supported because it uses an official count from a neighboring county and answers a likely objection, while Writer 2 relies on vague claims, a bandwagon appeal, and a slippery slope.”

notes.say: Have the student say what each thesis lacks before fixing it. Accept any strong thesis that names Writer 1, gives evidence-based reasons, and mentions Writer 2. Write the student's version on the board and polish it together.
ask: Which word in your thesis shows you are judging evidence, not sharing an opinion? (expected: “supported,” “relies on,” “official,” “vague”)
notes.answer: 1 is personal opinion; 2 takes no position; 3 gives no reasons and names only one writer. Sample thesis: “Writer 1's argument is better supported because it uses an official count from a neighboring county and answers a likely objection, while Writer 2 relies on vague claims, a bandwagon appeal, and a slippery slope.”
notes.watch: If the student's thesis lists reasons that are opinions (“because recycling is important”), ask, “Is that from the passage? What is the evidence?”

slides.title: Plan in 10 minutes
slides.board:
MinutesDo this
About 10Read both, highlight, fill the organizer, write the thesis
About 28Type the introduction, 2–3 body paragraphs, conclusion
About 7Reread; fix errors; check that both passages are used

Organizer rows (one column per passage): Claim · Key evidence · Quality · Flaws or appeals · Handles the other side?

notes.say: Students who start typing right away often wander and run out of time. Ten minutes of planning saves time later, because every paragraph already has a job. The organizer has two columns, one per passage, and neither column may be empty. Writing the thesis at the end of planning, before the introduction, is the key move. These times are a guide, not a rule; the point is to protect planning time and checking time.
ask: Why should neither column of the organizer be empty? (expected: the prompt requires evidence from both passages)
notes.watch: Students copy whole sentences into the organizer and lose time. Teach short notes with paragraph numbers: “team-paid study, 1,200 jobs (p. 2).”

slides.title: The ballpark organizer
slides.board:

steps: Thesis (from the Quality and Flaws rows): Osei is better supported because of independent research and specific cost figures; Bell relies on a team-paid study, one story, and pride.
Body 1: Bell's weak evidence: team-paid study, Harlan City story, “pay for itself.”
Body 2: Osei's strong evidence: independent studies, spending moves around, $77.5M vs. $400K.
Body 3: Bell's best point (lease) and Osei's answer (middle path). Conclusion: restate the thesis in new words.

notes.say: Build the organizer row by row with the student calling out entries. Then turn it into an essay map. Show how each row feeds a paragraph: Bell's column becomes body 1, Osei's column becomes body 2, and the “Other side?” row becomes body 3.
ask: Which row gives you the material for a fairness paragraph? (expected: the “Other side?” row)

slides.title: Body paragraphs: P-E-E-L
slides.board:
StepJobStarter
PointTopic sentence with a judgment“Bell's evidence is weaker than it looks.”
EvidenceQuote or paraphrase, with paragraph“He states that…”
ExplainWhy it is strong or weak“This shows… because…”
LinkBack to the thesis or the other passage“In contrast, Osei…”

Explain is where Trait 1 points are earned. Never leave a quote alone.

notes.say: P-E-E-L gives every body paragraph the same reliable shape. The Point is a judgment, not a summary. The Evidence is a short quote or paraphrase. The Explain step is the one students skip and the one that earns the most: say why the evidence is strong or weak using the five questions. The Link ties the paragraph back to the thesis or to the other passage. Repeat Evidence and Explain two or three times in one paragraph if there is more to say.
ask: What judgment words could start a Point sentence? (expected: strong, weak, reliable, biased, specific, vague, unsupported, credible)
notes.watch: Students write summary Points: “Bell talks about jobs.” Ask, “Is that a judgment? Is the evidence strong or weak?”

slides.title: Model response 1: the introduction
slides.board:
Port Delaney must decide whether to spend $48 million in public money on a downtown ballpark for the Pelicans, its minor league team. Marcus Bell, president of the Downtown Business Association, argues that the ballpark would bring jobs and life back to downtown. Dr. Elaine Osei, an economics professor, argues that the deal is a bad bet for taxpayers. Osei's position is better supported because she relies on independent research and specific cost figures, while Bell depends on a study paid for by the team, one secondhand story, and appeals to pride.

What does each sentence do?
steps: Sentence 1: the issue in plain words, with the key fact ($48 million).
Sentences 2–3: both authors, with their roles and positions, stated neutrally.
Sentence 4: the thesis: side (Osei), reasons (independent research, cost figures), and both authors (“while Bell…”).
No “I think,” no summary of every detail: just setup and a clear position.

notes.say: Here is the start of a model response that would earn 2 points on every trait. The full response is in the Student Lesson. Read it aloud, then reveal the annotations one at a time. Point out that the introduction is short. Its job is to set up the issue, introduce both authors fairly, and end with the thesis.
ask: Why include each author's job title? (expected: it introduces the sources and sets up the credibility discussion)

slides.title: Model response 2: the weaker side's evidence
slides.board:
Bell's strongest-sounding evidence is weaker than it first appears. He states that the ballpark would create 1,200 jobs, but this number comes from “a study commissioned by the Pelicans,” the team that would receive the new park. A source that profits from the result has a reason to make the numbers look good. Bell also points to his brother-in-law, who says downtown Harlan City is now “packed with new restaurants and apartments” after its 2015 stadium opened. One relative's impression of one city cannot prove what will happen in Port Delaney. In addition, Bell promises that the park “will pay for itself many times over” but offers no figures to show how. Finally, he leans on civic pride and on the claim that “everyone I talk to downtown is excited,” but popularity is not proof.

Find the P-E-E-L moves.
steps: Point: “Bell's strongest-sounding evidence is weaker than it first appears.” A judgment, not a summary.
Evidence + Explain 1: the 1,200 jobs come from “a study commissioned by the Pelicans” → a source that profits has a reason to inflate numbers (Source).
Evidence + Explain 2: the brother-in-law's “packed” Harlan City → one relative, one city cannot prove a pattern (Sufficient).
Evidence + Explain 3: “will pay for itself many times over” → no figures (Specific).

Evidence + Explain 4: civic pride and “everyone I talk to downtown is excited” → popularity is not proof (bandwagon). Every short quote is explained, and the paragraph covers each weakness the thesis promised.

notes.say: This body paragraph tests Bell's evidence one piece at a time. Reveal the labels one by one. Show that every quotation is followed by an explanation of why the evidence is weak, using the language of the five questions: source, sufficient, specific.
ask: Which transition words move the paragraph from one piece of evidence to the next? (expected: “also,” “In addition,” “Finally”)

slides.title: Model response 3: you label it
slides.board:
Osei, on the other hand, supports her claims with specific, checkable evidence. She reports that independent economists have studied stadiums “in dozens of cities over more than thirty years” and found that new stadiums “rarely produce meaningful growth in local jobs or income.” She also explains why: a family that spends $120 at a game usually spends that money instead of going out elsewhere in town, so “the spending moves around; it does not grow.” Her cost figures are just as clear. She calculates that the city would repay about $77.5 million over 25 years but collect only about $400,000 a year in rent. These numbers show that taxpayers would pay far more than they get back.

Label the Point, each Evidence, the Explain, and the Link.
steps: Point: “Osei, on the other hand, supports her claims with specific, checkable evidence.” (“On the other hand” also links to body 1.)
Evidence: the independent studies “in dozens of cities over more than thirty years”; the $120 family and “the spending moves around.”
Evidence: $77.5 million repaid over 25 years vs. about $400,000 a year in rent.
Explain: “These numbers show that taxpayers would pay far more than they get back.”

notes.say: Now the student does the labeling and you confirm. Ask them to read the paragraph and call out each P-E-E-L move. Then ask which sentence earns the most Trait 1 credit; the answer is the Explain sentence, because it judges what the numbers mean.
ask: Check the math: about $400,000 a year for 25 years is about how much? (expected: about $10 million, far less than $77.5 million)
notes.answer: Point: the first sentence. Evidence: the independent studies quote; the $120 family example with “the spending moves around”; the $77.5 million vs. $400,000 rent figures. Explain: “These numbers show that taxpayers would pay far more than they get back.” The opening “on the other hand” links back to body paragraph 1. $400,000 × 25 = $10 million.
notes.watch: If the student labels “She also explains why…” as Explain, clarify: that sentence reports Osei's reasoning (still Evidence). The essay writer's own Explain is the judgment at the end.

slides.title: Model response 4: fairness and conclusion
slides.board:
To be fair, Bell raises one real concern: the team's lease ends in two years, and the owners may move. However, Osei does not ignore this risk. She admits that losing the team “would disappoint many fans, me included,” and she proposes that the city offer the land and help with roads and parking while the owners pay most of the cost. Because she answers the other side instead of brushing it off, her argument is more credible.

In the end, Osei builds her case on independent research, clear numbers, and a fair answer to the opposing view, while Bell builds his on a team-funded study, a relative's opinion, and civic pride. For these reasons, Osei's argument is the better supported of the two.

Why admit Bell has a point?
steps: “To be fair” signals a counterargument: Bell's best point (the lease, the owners may move).
“However” turns to Osei's answer: she admits the loss and offers a middle path.
Explain: answering the other side makes her more credible, which supports the thesis.
Conclusion: the thesis in new words, comparing both authors one last time. No new evidence.

notes.say: The fourth paragraph surprises students: why praise the weaker side? Because a judge who admits the other side's best point and shows it is answered is more convincing. Then the conclusion restates the thesis in new words. It does not add new evidence.
ask: What would be lost if the essay skipped paragraph 4? (expected: it would look one-sided; the judgment would be less convincing)

slides.title: Your turn: test the evidence
slides.board:
Claim: Riverside should keep its public pools open until 9 p.m. in summer.

Strong or weak? Name the reason.

  1. “The parks department counted 1,450 swimmers after 6 p.m. during a two-week trial last July.”
  2. “My kids love night swimming, so every family in town will too.”
  3. “A survey by the company that would install the pool lights found that 90 percent of residents want later hours.”
  4. “If we close at 6, teenagers will have nowhere to go and the whole town will fall apart.”
steps: 1. Strong: named source, specific number, relevant to the claim.
2. Weak: hasty generalization from one family.
3. Weak: the source gains from the result (the lighting company).
4. Weak: slippery slope; no evidence for the chain of events.

notes.say: Start a three-minute timer and stay quiet. When time is up, the student gives a verdict and a reason for each before you reveal anything. Insist on naming the test or the flaw.
notes.answer: 1. Strong (named, specific, relevant). 2. Weak, hasty generalization. 3. Weak, biased source: the company profits if the pools stay open later. 4. Weak, slippery slope.
notes.watch: On item 3, students see “90 percent” and call it strong. Ask, “Who ran the survey, and what do they gain?”

slides.title: Your turn: thesis
slides.board:
Notes on a pool pair: Writer A (keep pools open late) cites the parks department count and a $9,000 staffing cost and adds two lifeguards to answer safety worries. Writer B (close at 6) uses one story, “everyone knows,” and a slippery slope.

  1. What is wrong with: “I love night swimming, so the pools should stay open”?
  2. What is wrong with: “Writer A's argument is better supported”?
  3. Write a strong thesis with the frame.
steps: 1. Personal opinion; it judges night swimming, not the writers.
2. Takes a side but gives no reasons and mentions only one writer.

3. Sample: “Writer A's argument is better supported because it uses a parks department count and real costs and answers the safety concern, while Writer B relies on one story, a bandwagon appeal, and a slippery slope.”

notes.say: Give the student four minutes. For problem 3, any thesis that names Writer A, gives evidence-based reasons, and mentions Writer B is correct. Have the student read it aloud, then check the three jobs together.
notes.answer: 1. Personal opinion, not a judgment of the arguments. 2. No reasons; only one writer. 3. Any thesis that does all three jobs, such as the sample.
notes.watch: If the thesis lists five reasons, it gets long and tangled. Two or three reasons per side is plenty.

slides.title: Your turn: P-E-E-L and traits
slides.board:
1. Label each sentence P, E, Explain, or L.

(a) Writer B's evidence is the weaker of the two. (b) She writes that “everyone knows pools are dangerous at night.” (c) This is a bandwagon appeal: it gives no accident numbers and no source. (d) Writer A, in contrast, uses the parks department's own count.

2. “Writer B's evidence is kinda weak cuz it aint got no numbers.” Which trait does this hurt, and how would you fix it?
steps: 1. (a) Point · (b) Evidence · (c) Explain · (d) Link
2. Mainly Trait 3 (“aint got no” is nonstandard), plus the formal tone in Trait 2 (“kinda,” “cuz”).
Fix: “Writer B's evidence is weak because it includes no numbers or sources.”

notes.say: Three minutes. For problem 2, the idea is fine but the language is informal and nonstandard. Formal tone is part of Trait 2, and grammar is Trait 3. Ask the student to say the fixed sentence aloud.
notes.answer: 1. (a) Point, (b) Evidence, (c) Explain, (d) Link. 2. Trait 3 (nonstandard grammar: “aint got no”) and Trait 2's formal style (“kinda,” “cuz”). Sample fix: “Writer B's evidence is weak because it includes no numbers or sources.”
notes.watch: If the student labels (d) as Point, ask whether it starts a new idea or connects to the other passage. A Link points to the thesis or the other side.

slides.title: GED question: most credible evidence
slides.board:
Which evidence from the ballpark passages is most credible?

A. Bell: a study commissioned by the Pelicans found 1,200 jobs.
B. Bell: his brother-in-law says downtown Harlan City is packed.
C. Osei: independent economists studied stadiums in dozens of cities over thirty years.
D. Bell: “Everyone I talk to downtown is excited.”
steps: A is out: the source is the team that gains from the result. Specific is not the same as reliable.
B is out: one relative's impression of one city is an anecdote, a hasty generalization.
D is out: a bandwagon appeal from an unnamed group; popularity is not proof.
C is correct: independent researchers, many cities, many years. It passes Source and Sufficient.

notes.say: Treat this like the real test. Have the student predict first: which of the five questions will decide it? Then eliminate one choice at a time, naming the flaw each time.
ask: Which of the five questions decides this item? (expected: Source, then Sufficient)
notes.answer: C. A has a biased source; B is an anecdote (hasty generalization); D is a bandwagon appeal.

slides.title: GED question: improve the paragraph
slides.board:
Osei's argument is better. She uses a lot of facts. Bell uses less facts. So Osei wins.

Which revision would most improve this paragraph's score?

A. Change “less” to “fewer.”
B. Add a quotation from each passage and explain why each piece of evidence is strong or weak.
C. Add a sentence about the writer's own feelings about baseball.
D. Repeat “Osei's argument is better” in different words to make the paragraph longer.
steps: A is a real fix (fewer for countable facts) but tiny: Trait 3 only.
C is out: personal feelings move the paragraph away from the task and hurt Trait 1.
D is out: repetition adds length, not support.
B is correct: specific evidence from both passages plus an explanation is exactly what Trait 1 rewards.

notes.say: This mirrors how scorers think. Ask the student which trait is weakest in the paragraph before looking at choices: Trait 1, because it never shows or explains any evidence.
ask: Why is “She uses a lot of facts” not enough? (expected: it does not show which facts or why they are reliable)
notes.answer: B. A fixes one small Trait 3 error; C adds personal opinion; D adds words but no evidence.

slides.title: GED strategy: thesis first, then type
slides.board:
1. Read the prompt and underline: both positions · best supported · both articles.
  2. Read and mark: strong evidence in one way, flaws in another.
  3. Organizer: two columns, short notes with paragraph numbers.
  4. Write the thesis with the frame before the introduction.
  5. Save 7 minutes to reread: both passages used? errors fixed?

If you cannot finish “___'s argument is better supported because ___, while ___ relies on ___,” go back to the passages for two more minutes.

notes.say: The single best habit for this essay is writing the thesis before writing anything else. If the student can complete the frame, the introduction's last line and the body paragraph topics are done. If they cannot, they are not ready to write, and two more minutes with the passages is far cheaper than rewriting a wandering essay. Remind them there is no spell-check, so the final reread matters.
ask: What will you do if 15 minutes have passed and you have no thesis? (expected: stop, reread the organizer, pick the side with stronger evidence, and write the thesis now)

slides.title: Recap and next steps
slides.board:
• The task: which side is better supported, not which you agree with.
  • 3 traits, 0–2 each (doubled, up to 12 RLA raw points): argument and evidence · development and organization · clarity and conventions.
  • Test evidence: source, specific, relevant, sufficient, fair. Specific ≠ reliable.
  • Thesis: side + reasons + both authors, at the end of the introduction.
  • Plan 10 minutes; build body paragraphs with P-E-E-L; Explain earns Trait 1.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice Set A (Set B if under 80%) → Exit Check

notes.say: Have the student say the five evidence questions and the three thesis jobs from memory before you reveal the recap. Then walk through what comes next: the Student Lesson repeats today step by step with the full model response and a check on every screen, Practice Set A uses two new passages about artificial turf, and the Exit Check confirms readiness for week 10, where we write, revise, and edit a full timed response.
ask: What is one thing you will do differently on the Extended Response because of today? (expected: any specific habit, such as writing the thesis first or explaining every quote)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, you will write one essay, called the Extended Response. You get 45 minutes to read two passages that take opposite sides on an issue and type a response about them. It is worth up to 12 raw points on the RLA test, and it rewards a clear method. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • explain what the Extended Response asks and how it is scored on three traits, each worth 0 to 2 points
  • test evidence with five questions: source, specific, relevant, sufficient, and fair
  • decide which of two arguments is better supported, using evidence instead of opinion
  • write a thesis that names the better-supported side, gives reasons, and mentions both authors
  • plan in about 10 minutes and build body paragraphs with P-E-E-L

You will study one pair of passages about a ballpark all the way through, ending with a full model response and notes on why it scores well. Most screens end with a check. Answer it before you move on.

screens.title: The task: be the judge
screens.html:
Every Extended Response prompt looks like this:

In your response, analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from both articles to support your response.

Read it closely. It does not ask what you think about the issue. It asks which author did a better job of proving their position. Think of yourself as a judge in a debate: you may personally prefer one side, but your ruling is based on the proof each side brings.

  • Analyze both positions: discuss both authors.
  • Which one is best supported: choose one side, based on evidence.
  • Evidence from both articles: show the strengths of one and the weaknesses of the other.

You can disagree with the better-supported side and still earn a top score.

check.prompt: A student plans to begin an Extended Response about a proposed ballpark with this sentence: “I believe the city should build the ballpark because baseball brings people together.” What is the main problem with this plan?
check.hint: Reread the prompt. Does it ask what you think about the issue, or something else?
check.explain: The prompt asks which position is best supported. “I believe the city should build the ballpark” responds to a different question: what the student wants. The reason, “baseball brings people together,” comes from the student, not from either passage. The most tempting wrong answer says to stay neutral, but the essay must pick a side; it just has to pick it based on the evidence.
options: It argues the student's own view of the issue instead of judging which author better supports a position.
It takes a side, but a GED response should stay neutral and avoid choosing either author's position.
It is too short, because a GED opening sentence must list at least four separate reasons from the passages.
It agrees with the author who supports the proposal, and GED scorers expect writers to side against new proposals.
why: The response must choose a side; the prompt asks which position is best supported. What it must avoid is choosing based on personal opinion.
There is no rule about the number of reasons in an opening sentence. The problem is what kind of reason it gives: a personal belief, not evidence from the passages.
Scorers do not prefer either side. Either position can earn full credit if the essay proves it is better supported. The real problem is that the sentence gives the student's opinion of baseball.

screens.title: The three traits
screens.html:
Trained scorers read your essay and give it 0, 1, or 2 points on each of three traits.

TraitWhat scorers look for
1. Creation of arguments and use of evidenceA clear position on which argument is better supported; specific, relevant evidence from both passages; an explanation of why the evidence is strong or weak
2. Development of ideas and organizational structureAn introduction, body paragraphs, and a conclusion; ideas that build in a logical order, joined by clear transitions; each paragraph with a clear job; precise word choice; a formal style and a serious tone
3. Clarity and command of standard English conventionsClear, varied sentence structure; no run-ons, fragments, or awkward sentences; mostly correct grammar, usage, spelling, capitalization, and punctuation

Trait 1 is about your thinking, Trait 2 is about the shape of the essay, and Trait 3 is about your sentences.

check.prompt: Drag each description into the trait it belongs to.
check.hint: Ask: is this about my reasoning (Trait 1), the shape and tone of my essay (Trait 2), or my sentences (Trait 3)?
check.explain: Trait 1 is about the argument: a clear position and evidence from both passages with an explanation. Trait 2 is about structure and style: introduction, body, conclusion, and a formal tone. Trait 3 is about sentence-level correctness: grammar, spelling, punctuation, and complete sentences.
choices: Writes clear sentences with no run-ons or fragments
Uses correct grammar, spelling, capitalization, and punctuation
Keeps a formal, serious tone from start to finish
Organizes the essay into an introduction, body paragraphs, and a conclusion
Takes a clear position on which argument is better supported
Uses specific evidence from both passages and explains why it is strong or weak
check.why: The most common mistake is putting “explains why evidence is strong or weak” under Trait 2 because it sounds like developing ideas. Judging the evidence is the heart of the argument, so it belongs to Trait 1. Students also put “formal tone” under Trait 3; tone is part of Trait 2.

screens.title: What earns 2, 1, or 0
screens.html:
On each trait, 2 means the skill is strong, 1 means it is partly there, and 0 means it is missing or very weak. Some examples for Trait 1:

  • 2: picks the better-supported side, uses specific evidence from both passages, and explains why it is strong or weak.
  • 1: picks a side but uses thin evidence, uses only one passage, or quotes without explaining.
  • 0: gives only a personal opinion or barely connects to the passages.

An essay that is off topic, copies large parts of the passages, or is left blank can receive no credit at all. Always write something, and always write about the passages.

How it counts: your three trait scores add up to 0–6 points, and the GED doubles that total. So the essay is worth up to 12 raw points on the RLA test, roughly a fifth of the test's raw points.

Scorers know you are writing a first draft in 45 minutes. A few small errors will not cost you Trait 3 points. Errors that make sentences hard to understand will.

check.prompt: Each of the three traits is scored 0, 1, or 2. What is the highest total number of trait points an essay can earn? Type the number.
check.hint: Multiply the number of traits by the top score on each trait.
check.explain: There are three traits, and each one can earn a maximum of 2 points: 3 × 2 = 6. Typing 2 is the most common mistake: that is the maximum for a single trait. (The GED later doubles the 6 trait points to 12 raw points, but the trait total itself is 6.)

mistakes.why: 2 is the most one trait can earn. There are three traits, and each can earn 2 points.
3 is the number of traits, not the number of points. Each of the three traits can earn up to 2 points.
Each of the 3 traits can earn up to 2 points, and 3 × 2 = 6, not 4. Check that you counted all three traits.
12 is what the GED counts after it doubles the trait total. The question asks for trait points: 3 traits × 2 points = 6.

screens.title: Test the evidence: five questions
screens.html:
Evidence is whatever an author uses to prove a claim: facts, numbers, studies, examples, expert statements, or stories. Not all evidence is equal. Test each important piece with five questions:

  1. Source: Who says so? Are they an expert? Are they named? Do they gain anything from the result?
  2. Specific: Are there numbers, dates, measurements, or named studies? Or vague words like “many” and “everyone”?
  3. Relevant: Does it prove this claim, or something next to it?
  4. Sufficient: Is there enough? One story is not a pattern.
  5. Fair: Does the author deal honestly with the other side?

Specific is not the same as reliable. A precise number from a source that profits from the result can still be weak evidence.

example.prompt: A gym advertises: “In our own survey of 400 members, 82 percent said they plan to renew.” Is this strong evidence that the gym is good?
steps: Specific: yes, 400 members and 82 percent.
Sufficient: 400 people is a real sample, much better than one person's opinion.
Source: the gym ran its own survey and gains from good results, so the numbers may be slanted.
example.answer: Better than an opinion, but not fully reliable: it fails the Source question.

check.prompt: An article supports its claim with “a survey paid for by the company that sells the product.” Which of the five evidence questions raises the biggest concern? Type one word.
check.hint: Who produced the evidence, and what do they gain?
check.explain: The company that sells the product paid for the survey, so it gains from good results. That is a Source problem: the source may be biased. A survey can be specific and still unreliable.

mistakes.why: The survey may well include exact numbers, so it could pass Specific. The concern is who paid for it: the company gains from good results.
Fair is about how the author treats the other side of the argument. Here the concern is who produced the evidence.
Sufficient asks whether there is enough evidence. The problem here is not the amount; it is that the company that ran the survey profits from the result.

screens.title: Red flags: faulty reasoning
screens.html:
Some arguments sound convincing but rest on faulty reasoning. Learn to name these:

Red flagWhat it doesExample
Hasty generalizationOne or two cases become a rule“It worked in one city, so it will work everywhere.”
BandwagonPopularity is treated as proof“Everyone I know supports it.”
Slippery slopeOne step will lead to disaster, with no proof“If we allow this, soon we'll lose everything.”
Emotional appealFeelings replace evidence“Think of the children!” with no facts
Unsupported claimA big claim with no source or numbers“It will pay for itself many times over.”

Naming the flaw gives you precise words for your essay. “Bell relies on a hasty generalization” earns more than “Bell is wrong.”

check.prompt:
Name the faulty reasoning in each statement.

“If the city lowers the speed limit, next it will ban cars from downtown.” This is {{0}}.

“Every parent I know supports the new school schedule, so it must be the right choice.” This is {{1}}.

“My neighbor's solar panels broke after a year, so solar power does not work.” This is {{2}}.
check.hint: Ask: is it a chain of events, popularity used as proof, or one case turned into a rule?
check.explain: (1) One step (a lower speed limit) is said to lead to an extreme result (banning cars) with no proof: slippery slope. (2) Support from “every parent I know” is used as proof: bandwagon. (3) One neighbor's experience becomes a rule about all solar power: hasty generalization.

options: a hasty generalization
a bandwagon appeal
a slippery slope
why: A hasty generalization draws a rule from too few examples. This statement predicts that one step will lead to an extreme result, which is a slippery slope.
A bandwagon appeal points to how many people support something. This statement predicts a chain of events with no proof that one step leads to the next.

options: a bandwagon appeal
a slippery slope
a hasty generalization
why: A slippery slope predicts a chain of worse and worse events. This statement uses popularity (“every parent I know”) as proof.
It is based on a small group, but the reasoning is “many people support it, so it is right.” That is a bandwagon appeal.

options: a slippery slope
a bandwagon appeal
a hasty generalization
why: A slippery slope predicts a chain of events. This statement takes one case (one neighbor's panels) and makes a rule about all solar power.
Nobody's opinion or popularity is mentioned. The flaw is drawing a rule about all solar power from one example.

screens.title: The ballpark pair: Passage A
screens.html:
Read Passage A. As you read, mark strong evidence one way and weak evidence or appeals another way.

Passage A: Build the Ballpark and Bring Downtown Back

By Marcus Bell, President, Port Delaney Downtown Business Association

[1] For twenty years, the old rail yard on Front Street has sat empty behind a chain-link fence. The Port Delaney Pelicans, our minor league baseball team, have offered to move into a new downtown ballpark there if the city provides $48 million to build it. The city council should say yes.

[2] A study commissioned by the Pelicans found that the new ballpark would create 1,200 jobs and bring $30 million a year into the local economy. Restaurants and shops near the park would be full every game night.

[3] We have all seen what a ballpark can do. My brother-in-law lives in Harlan City, which opened a new stadium in 2015. He says downtown Harlan City is now packed with new restaurants and apartments. If it worked for Harlan City, it will work for us.

[4] The team's lease ends in two years, and the owners have said publicly that they will consider offers from other cities. Losing our team would be a blow to the city's pride.

[5] Some critics complain about the cost. But the ballpark will pay for itself many times over. Everyone I talk to downtown is excited, and Port Delaney deserves a city it can be proud of.

check.prompt: Which statement best expresses Bell's main claim in Passage A?
check.hint: Look at the end of paragraph 1, where Bell tells the council what to do.
check.explain: Bell states his claim at the end of paragraph 1: the Pelicans will move into a new downtown ballpark “if the city provides $48 million to build it. The city council should say yes.” The rest of the passage gives his reasons. The owners-pay choice is tempting if you mix up the passages: that idea comes from Osei.
options: Port Delaney should study Harlan City's stadium before choosing a ballpark site.
The city should turn the old rail yard on Front Street into a shopping district.
The Pelicans' owners should pay to build a new ballpark on the Front Street land.
The city should pay $48 million to build a downtown ballpark for the Pelicans.
why: Bell uses Harlan City as an example of success. He never asks for a study; he says “If it worked for Harlan City, it will work for us.”
The rail yard is where the ballpark would go. Bell never proposes a shopping district; he predicts shops near the park would be busy.
Bell wants the city to provide the $48 million. Owners paying most of the cost is Osei's middle path in Passage B, not Bell's claim.

screens.title: The ballpark pair: Passage B
screens.html:
Now read Passage B, which answers Passage A. Mark it the same way.

Passage B: A Ballpark Is a Bad Bet for Taxpayers

By Dr. Elaine Osei, Professor of Economics, Port Delaney Community College

[1] A downtown ballpark sounds exciting, and I understand why many residents want one. But before the council commits $48 million in public money, residents should look at the evidence.

[2] Independent economists have studied publicly funded stadiums in dozens of cities over more than thirty years. They have reached a consistent conclusion: new stadiums rarely produce meaningful growth in local jobs or income. Most fans are local residents, so a family that spends $120 at a ballgame usually spends that money instead of going to a movie or a restaurant elsewhere in town. The spending moves around; it does not grow.

[3] The study the Pelicans paid for claims 1,200 jobs. Yet the team plays about 70 home games a year, and most ballpark jobs are part-time and seasonal. The study never says how many of the jobs would be full-time.

[4] To raise the $48 million, the city would repay about $3.1 million a year for 25 years, about $77.5 million in all. The proposed lease would return only about $400,000 a year in rent.

[5] Losing the Pelicans would disappoint many fans, me included. But if the team benefits from a new park, the owners should pay most of the cost, while the city offers the land and helps with roads and parking.

check.prompt: Bell says the ballpark would create 1,200 jobs. Click the sentence that gives Osei's reason for doubting that those jobs would be steady, year-round work.
check.hint: Look in paragraph 3, where Osei responds to the team's study.
check.explain: In paragraph 3, Osei answers the 1,200-jobs claim directly: “Yet the team plays about 70 home games a year, and most ballpark jobs are part-time and seasonal.” Seventy games a year means the jobs exist only part of the time. The other sentences are about spending, rent, or her own feelings, not the kind of jobs.
spans: A downtown ballpark sounds exciting, and I understand why many residents want one.
Most fans are local residents, so a family that spends $120 at a ballgame usually spends that money instead of going to a movie or a restaurant elsewhere in town.
Yet the team plays about 70 home games a year, and most ballpark jobs are part-time and seasonal.
The proposed lease would return only about $400,000 a year in rent.
Losing the Pelicans would disappoint many fans, me included.
check.why: Many students click the $120 family sentence because it is about the economy. That sentence explains why spending does not grow; it does not explain why the jobs would not be steady. The 70-games sentence is the one about the jobs themselves.

screens.title: Testing Bell's evidence
screens.html:
Now put the five questions to work. Bell's most impressive-sounding evidence is in paragraph 2: “A study commissioned by the Pelicans found that the new ballpark would create 1,200 jobs and bring $30 million a year into the local economy.”

Always check the other passage too. A strong essay uses one passage to show what the other leaves out.

steps: Source: “commissioned by the Pelicans” means the team paid for it, and the team gets the ballpark. The source gains from the result.
Specific: yes, it has numbers. That makes it sound strong.
Check the other passage: Osei notes the team plays about 70 home games a year, most ballpark jobs are part-time and seasonal, and the study never says how many jobs would be full-time.
example.answer: Weak. The numbers come from a source with a stake in the outcome, and Passage B shows what they leave out.

check.prompt: Why is Bell's evidence about Harlan City (paragraph 3) weak?
check.hint: Who is the source, how many cases does it cover, and are there any numbers?
check.explain: The Harlan City evidence fails the Sufficient test: it is one relative's description of one city. It also fails Specific, since it has no numbers, and it never shows that the stadium caused the change. Turning one example into a rule (“If it worked for Harlan City, it will work for us”) is a hasty generalization. The team-paid-study choice is tempting, but it describes Bell's paragraph 2 evidence, not paragraph 3.
options: It gives exact counts of new restaurants and apartments, but Bell does not say where the counts came from.
It is one relative's impression of one city, so it cannot show a pattern or prove the stadium caused the change.
It comes from a study the Pelicans paid for, so the team had a reason to exaggerate the stadium's success.
It describes a stadium that opened in 2015, which is too long ago to tell us anything about Port Delaney.
why: Bell gives no counts at all. His brother-in-law only says downtown is “packed.” Check the passage before accepting a detail.
That is the problem with Bell's job numbers in paragraph 2. The Harlan City evidence comes from his brother-in-law, not from a study.
The date is not the problem; a 2015 stadium could give useful evidence. The problem is that the evidence is one person's impression of one city.

screens.title: Which side is better supported?
screens.html:
To reach a verdict, fill in a simple scorecard for each passage: its best evidence, its weakest evidence, its red flags, and how it handles the other side. Then compare.

The better-supported side is the one whose key evidence survives the five questions and who deals fairly with the other side. It does not have to be perfect.

Do not decide by length, emotion, confidence, or which side you agree with. And do not assume the side arguing “no” always wins.

steps: Bell: best evidence is a team-paid study; also an anecdote, a bandwagon appeal (“Everyone I talk to”), and an unsupported promise (“pay for itself”). He waves off cost critics.

Osei: independent studies over 30 years; a clear reason spending does not grow; checkable costs ($3.1 million × 25 years = $77.5 million vs. $400,000 a year in rent). One gap: she does not name the studies.
Other side: Osei admits losing the team would hurt and offers a middle path.

check.skill: Deciding which side is better supported
check.prompt: Which two statements best explain why Osei's argument is better supported than Bell's? Select two answers.
check.hint: Look for reasons that use the five evidence questions, not reasons about length, position, or title.
check.explain: Osei's key evidence passes the Source test (independent economists, not the team), and she passes the Fair test by admitting the cost of losing the team and proposing a middle path. The “more numbers” choice is tempting, but quantity is not quality: Bell's numbers are specific too, and they still fail the Source test.
options: She answers the other side by admitting fans would be disappointed and offering a middle path.
Her passage uses more numbers than Bell's, and the side with more numbers always wins.
She argues against spending the money, and arguments against a proposal are usually stronger.
She is a professor, so readers can accept what she says without testing her evidence.
Her research comes from independent economists, while Bell's job numbers come from a study the team paid for.
why: Counting numbers is not enough; what matters is whether the numbers are reliable. Bell has numbers too (1,200 jobs, $30 million), but they come from a biased source.
Neither side wins because of its position. In this week's turf practice, the side arguing “yes” is better supported. Judge the evidence.
Credentials help, but you still test the evidence. Osei wins because her evidence passes the five questions, not because of her title alone.

screens.title: Writing a thesis
screens.html:
Your thesis is the one sentence your whole essay proves. On the Extended Response it has three jobs:

  1. Name the side that is better supported.
  2. Give the reasons, based on evidence.
  3. Mention both authors.

Frame: ___'s argument is better supported because ___, while ___ relies on ___.

Put it at the end of your introduction. It is also your outline: the “because” part becomes one body paragraph and the “while … relies on” part becomes another.

example.prompt: Climb the thesis ladder for the ballpark pair.
steps: “I think a ballpark is a waste of money.” Personal opinion; no passages.
“Both authors make good points.” No position.
“Osei's argument is better supported.” A side, but no reasons and only one author.
example.answer: “Osei's argument is better supported because she relies on independent research and specific cost figures, while Bell relies on a team-funded study, one personal story, and appeals to pride.” All three jobs.

check.prompt: Which thesis statement would best begin a high-scoring response to the ballpark passages?
check.hint: Check each choice for the three jobs: a side, evidence-based reasons, and both authors.
check.explain: The correct thesis names the side (Osei), gives evidence-based reasons (independent research, cost figures), and mentions both authors (“while Bell relies on…”). The professor choice is the most tempting because it chooses Osei, but its reason is a credential and a stereotype, not her evidence.
options: I think Port Delaney should not build the ballpark, because spending $48 million of taxpayer money on a baseball team is a waste when the city has other needs.
Osei's argument is better supported because she uses independent research and clear cost figures, while Bell relies on a team-paid study and a relative's story.
The ballpark debate matters to everyone in Port Delaney, and both Bell and Osei raise thoughtful points that the city council should weigh carefully before it votes.
Osei's argument is better supported because she is a professor with an advanced degree, and professors usually know more about money than business owners like Bell do.
why: This is the student's own opinion about the ballpark. It never says which author is better supported or mentions either one.
This takes no position. Fairness belongs in the body of the essay, but the thesis must name the better-supported side.
This picks the right side for the wrong reason. A job title is not evidence from the passage, and the claim about business owners is a generalization.

screens.title: Where the thesis goes
screens.html:
A strong introduction is short, usually three to five sentences:

  1. The issue, in plain words.
  2. Both authors and their positions, stated neutrally.
  3. Your thesis, as the last sentence.

Do not open with a long story or a dictionary definition, and do not save your position for the end of the essay. The scorer should know your verdict by the end of the first paragraph.

Write the thesis in your planning notes first. Then the introduction is easy: issue, authors, thesis.

check.prompt: Here is an introduction about the bottle-deposit pair from the lesson. Click the thesis statement.
check.hint: Find the sentence that does all three thesis jobs.
check.explain: The thesis is the last sentence: it names the better-supported side (Writer 1), gives reasons (an official count, answering an objection), and mentions both writers. The earlier sentences introduce the issue and each writer's position neutrally. “Both writers clearly care about their community” is a fair comment, but it takes no position.
spans: Ashford is debating whether to add a 10-cent deposit on bottles and cans.
Writer 1 argues that a deposit would clean up roadsides, pointing to results in neighboring Glen Ridge County.
Writer 2 argues that the deposit is a tax on working families.
Both writers clearly care about their community.
Writer 1's argument is better supported because it relies on an official count and answers a likely objection, while Writer 2 relies on vague claims and a slippery slope.
check.why: Some students click the sentence about Writer 1's position because it mentions evidence. That sentence only reports what Writer 1 argues; it does not judge which writer is better supported.

screens.title: Plan with an organizer
screens.html:
Spend about 10 minutes planning. Draw a two-column organizer, one column per passage, and fill it with short notes and paragraph numbers.

Bell (A)Osei (B)
ClaimCity should pay $48 millionCity should not; owners pay most
Key evidenceTeam study, 1,200 jobs (p. 2); Harlan City (p. 3); lease ends (p. 4)Independent studies; $120 family (p. 2); 70 games (p. 3); $77.5M vs. $400K (p. 4)
QualityWeak: biased source, one storyStrong: independent, checkable
Flaws or appealsHasty generalization; bandwagon; no figuresStudies not named
Other side?Waves off cost criticsAdmits loss; middle path

Neither column may be empty: the prompt requires evidence from both passages.

check.prompt: A student is filling in the Bell column of the organizer. Drag each note into the row where it belongs.
check.hint: Claim = what the author wants. Key evidence = facts offered as proof. Flaws = names for weak reasoning.
check.explain: Claim: what Bell wants, the city paying $48 million. Key evidence: the team-paid study and the lease, the facts Bell offers as proof. Flaws or appeals: the bandwagon line and the hasty generalization about Harlan City, which name what is wrong with his reasoning.
choices: Hasty generalization: one city's story treated as proof
Bandwagon: “Everyone I talk to downtown is excited”
Team-paid study: 1,200 jobs and $30 million a year (para. 2)
Lease ends in two years; owners may consider other cities (para. 4)
The city should pay $48 million for a downtown ballpark.
check.why: The most common mistake is putting the lease note under Flaws because it is an appeal to pride in the passage. The lease ending is a real, checkable fact, Bell's best evidence, so it goes under Key evidence.

screens.title: Your 45 minutes and your essay map
screens.html:
MinutesStep
About 10Read both passages, mark them, fill in the organizer, write your thesis
About 28Type the introduction, 2–3 body paragraphs, and a conclusion
About 7Reread: both passages used? errors fixed?

A reliable essay map:

  1. Introduction: issue, both authors, thesis.
  2. Body 1: the weaker side's evidence and why it fails.
  3. Body 2: the stronger side's evidence and why it holds up.
  4. Body 3 (optional): the weaker side's best point and how the stronger side answers it.
  5. Conclusion: the thesis in new words.

check.prompt: After 10 minutes of planning, a student has written this thesis: “Osei's argument is better supported because she relies on independent research and clear cost figures, while Bell relies on a team-paid study and a relative's story.” Which essay map fits this thesis best?
check.hint: Which map uses both passages, judges the evidence, and follows the two parts of the thesis?
check.explain: The thesis has a “because” part (Osei's strengths) and a “while” part (Bell's weaknesses), so the map gives each its own body paragraph, adds a fairness paragraph, and ends with a conclusion. The summary map is the most tempting because it uses both passages, but summarizing is not evaluating, and personal views do not answer the prompt.
options: Introduction with thesis; Bell's weak evidence; Osei's strong evidence; Bell's best point and Osei's answer; conclusion
Introduction; a summary of Bell's passage; a summary of Osei's passage; a conclusion giving the student's own view on stadiums
Begin the body paragraphs right away without an introduction, then write the thesis last once the essay's direction is clear
Introduction; three paragraphs on Osei's evidence; conclusion. Bell's passage can be skipped because it is the weaker one
why: Summaries retell the passages instead of judging them, and ending with the student's own view leaves the task. Each body paragraph needs a judgment.
The thesis is already written and should end the introduction. Writing it last risks an essay that wanders.
The prompt requires evidence from both articles. The weaker passage's flaws are half of your proof.

screens.title: Body paragraphs: P-E-E-L
screens.html:
Build each body paragraph with four moves:

MoveJob
PointA topic sentence with a judgment (strong, weak, reliable, biased)
EvidenceA short quote or paraphrase from the passage
ExplainWhy the evidence is strong or weak, using the five questions
LinkA connection back to the thesis or to the other passage

Explain is where you earn Trait 1 points. Never leave a quotation alone. You can repeat Evidence and Explain two or three times in one paragraph.

example.prompt: Build a P-E-E-L paragraph about Writer 1 in the bottle-deposit pair.
steps: Point: Writer 1 supports the deposit with official evidence.
Evidence: Writer 1 reports that Glen Ridge County's public works department counted 58 percent fewer bottles and cans along roadsides by 2022, three years after its deposit began.
Explain: This evidence is strong because it comes from a named public agency, uses a specific measurement, and describes a neighboring county.
example.answer: Link: Writer 2, in contrast, offers only what “everyone knows.”

check.prompt: Read this body paragraph about the ballpark pair. Click the sentence that does the Explain job.
check.hint: The Explain sentence answers “So what? Why does this evidence matter?”
check.explain: The first sentence is the Point (a judgment). The second gives the Evidence (the study and who paid for it). The third Explains why that matters: the team gains from the result, so the study may be biased. The last sentence Links to Osei.
spans: Bell's job numbers are not as reliable as they look.
He reports that a study found the ballpark would create 1,200 jobs, but the study was “commissioned by the Pelicans.”
Because the team would get the new ballpark, it had a reason to want large numbers, so the study may be biased.
Osei, by contrast, relies on independent economists who have nothing to gain.
check.why: Many students click the sentence with the quotation because it mentions who paid for the study. That sentence presents the evidence. The Explain sentence is the next one, which says why that fact makes the study unreliable.

screens.title: Model response, part 1
screens.html:
Here is a response to the ballpark pair that would earn 2 points on every trait.

[1] Port Delaney must decide whether to spend $48 million in public money on a downtown ballpark for the Pelicans, its minor league team. Marcus Bell, president of the Downtown Business Association, argues that the ballpark would bring jobs and life back to downtown. Dr. Elaine Osei, an economics professor, argues that the deal is a bad bet for taxpayers. Osei's position is better supported because she relies on independent research and specific cost figures, while Bell depends on a study paid for by the team, one secondhand story, and appeals to pride.

[2] Bell's strongest-sounding evidence is weaker than it first appears. He states that the ballpark would create 1,200 jobs, but this number comes from “a study commissioned by the Pelicans,” the team that would receive the new park. A source that profits from the result has a reason to make the numbers look good. Bell also points to his brother-in-law, who says downtown Harlan City is now “packed with new restaurants and apartments” after its 2015 stadium opened. One relative's impression of one city cannot prove what will happen in Port Delaney. In addition, Bell promises that the park “will pay for itself many times over” but offers no figures to show how. Finally, he leans on civic pride and on the claim that “everyone I talk to downtown is excited,” but popularity is not proof.

example.prompt: How do these two paragraphs earn points?
steps: Paragraph 1: issue ($48 million), both authors with roles and positions, then the thesis as the last sentence. Side, reasons, and both authors: Trait 1.
Paragraph 2, Point: “Bell's strongest-sounding evidence is weaker than it first appears.” A judgment, not a summary.

Paragraph 2, Evidence and Explain ×4: team-paid study → source gains from the result; brother-in-law's “packed” → one city cannot prove a pattern; “pay for itself” → no figures; civic pride and “everyone I talk to” → popularity is not proof. Every quote is explained, and every weakness named in the thesis is covered.
Style: formal tone, short quotations, transitions (“also,” “In addition,” “Finally”): Traits 2 and 3.
example.answer: Each paragraph has one job, and every piece of evidence is judged.

check.prompt: In paragraph 1 of the model response, what is the job of the last sentence?
check.hint: Look at the final sentence of paragraph 1. Which of the thesis jobs does it do?
check.explain: The last sentence is the thesis: “Osei's position is better supported because she relies on independent research and specific cost figures, while Bell depends on a study paid for by the team, one secondhand story, and appeals to pride.” It names the side, gives reasons, and previews the body paragraphs. The tempting “who wrote each passage” choice describes sentences 2 and 3, not the last one.
options: It tells readers who wrote each passage and what each author's job is so they can judge the sources.
It states which position is better supported and previews the reasons the body paragraphs will develop.
It admits that Bell makes one fair point before the essay turns to the evidence for Osei's side.
It gives the writer's personal opinion about whether Port Delaney really needs a new ballpark.
why: That is the job of the second and third sentences, which introduce Bell and Osei with their roles.
The fair point about Bell (the lease) comes in paragraph 4. The last sentence of paragraph 1 is the thesis.
The last sentence judges the two arguments; it never says whether the city needs a ballpark.

screens.title: Model response, part 2
screens.html:
[3] Osei, on the other hand, supports her claims with specific, checkable evidence. She reports that independent economists have studied stadiums “in dozens of cities over more than thirty years” and found that new stadiums “rarely produce meaningful growth in local jobs or income.” She also explains why: a family that spends $120 at a game usually spends that money instead of going out elsewhere in town, so “the spending moves around; it does not grow.” Her cost figures are just as clear. She calculates that the city would repay about $77.5 million over 25 years but collect only about $400,000 a year in rent. These numbers show that taxpayers would pay far more than they get back.

[4] To be fair, Bell raises one real concern: the team's lease ends in two years, and the owners may move. However, Osei does not ignore this risk. She admits that losing the team “would disappoint many fans, me included,” and she proposes that the city offer the land and help with roads and parking while the owners pay most of the cost. Because she answers the other side instead of brushing it off, her argument is more credible.

[5] In the end, Osei builds her case on independent research, clear numbers, and a fair answer to the opposing view, while Bell builds his on a team-funded study, a relative's opinion, and civic pride. For these reasons, Osei's argument is the better supported of the two.

steps: Paragraph 3: “On the other hand” links to paragraph 2. Evidence: the independent studies, the $120 family, and the cost figures. Explain: “These numbers show that taxpayers would pay far more than they get back.”
Paragraph 4: “To be fair” admits Bell's best point; “However” shows Osei's answer. Admitting and answering the other side makes the verdict more convincing.
Paragraph 5: restates the thesis in new words. No new evidence.
example.answer: Together: a clear position, evidence from both passages, a logical order, and clear sentences.

check.prompt: Why does the model response include paragraph 4, about Bell's point that the team might leave?
check.hint: Read the last sentence of paragraph 4. What does it say about Osei's argument?
check.explain: Paragraph 4 is a counterargument paragraph. It admits Bell's strongest point (the lease ends and the owners may move), then shows that Osei answers it with a middle path. A judge who deals with the other side's best point is more convincing than one who ignores it. The equal-space choice is tempting, but there is no such rule; the paragraph is there to strengthen the verdict.
options: Showing the other side's best point and how Osei answers it makes the essay's verdict more convincing.
The GED requires every essay to give exactly equal space to both passages, so the paragraph balances the essay.
It brings in a new fact about the lease from outside the passages, which shows the scorer some outside knowledge.
The writer has changed her mind by paragraph 4 and now thinks Bell's argument is the better supported one.
why: There is no equal-space rule. The essay must use evidence from both passages, but the amount depends on what the evidence shows.
The lease fact comes from Bell's paragraph 4, not from outside the passages. The essay should rely on the passages, not outside knowledge.
The paragraph ends by saying Osei's argument “is more credible,” and the conclusion still names Osei. The verdict has not changed.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
Here are the rules to carry into Practice:
