  • The Extended Response asks which argument is better supported, not which side you agree with.
  • Three traits, each 0–2: (1) argument and evidence, (2) development and organization (including transitions, word choice, and formal tone), (3) clarity and conventions (including sentence structure). The 0–6 total is doubled, up to 12 RLA raw points.
  • Test evidence with five questions: source, specific, relevant, sufficient, fair. Specific is not the same as reliable.
  • Name the red flags: hasty generalization, bandwagon, slippery slope, emotional appeal, unsupported claim.
  • Thesis = side + reasons + both authors, at the end of the introduction.
  • Plan about 10 minutes with a two-column organizer; use evidence from both passages.
  • Build body paragraphs with P-E-E-L; the Explain step earns Trait 1 points.

Next: Practice Set A (15 questions) on two new passages about artificial turf. Score 80% or higher on first tries to master it; otherwise take Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

stimuli.title: Passage A: More Playing Time for Millbrook: Why Corbin Park Needs Turf Fields
stimuli.html:
By Dana Whitfield, Director, Millbrook Parks and Recreation Department

[1] Every spring, the same scene plays out at Corbin Park. Parents pull into the parking lot, children pile out with their cleats on, and they find a sign taped to the gate: FIELDS CLOSED, TOO WET. The city council will soon vote on a plan to convert the park’s two main grass fields to artificial turf. I urge the council to approve it. Turf would give our young people far more time to play, and it would save water and money.

[2] Grass fields have served Millbrook well for decades, but they have a serious limit. When grass is wet, cleats tear up the roots, so the fields must close after heavy rain. Last year, the two main fields at Corbin Park were closed on 46 days, mostly during the spring and fall league seasons. Every closure means canceled practices, rescheduled games, and frustrated families. An artificial turf field drains quickly and can be used again within an hour of a storm.

[3] Because grass needs time to recover, we also limit how many hours each field can be used. Our department’s scheduling records show that the two fields were available for about 1,100 hours of play last year. With turf, we could schedule them for more than 3,000 hours. That extra time matters. This fall, our youth soccer and football leagues turned away 210 children because there was no field space for more teams.

[4] Turf would also save resources. Last summer, the two fields used 1.3 million gallons of water, during a season when residents were asked to limit lawn watering. Mowing, fertilizing, lining, and reseeding the two fields cost the city $58,000. Turf fields need brushing and cleaning, which we estimate at about $12,000 a year, for savings of roughly $46,000 a year.

[5] I want to be honest about the drawbacks. Turf is not cheap. The conversion will cost $2.2 million, and a regional recreation grant will cover half. A turf surface also wears out and must be replaced after about ten years, at a cost of about $450,000 per field. Our yearly savings would cover about half of that future cost, not all of it.

[6] Turf also gets hotter than grass in direct summer sun. We plan to address this in three ways: using a light-colored infill that stays cooler than black rubber, adding shade structures beside both fields, and having staff check the surface temperature with a handheld thermometer on summer afternoons. If the surface reaches 120 degrees, play will pause until it cools.

[7] No playing surface is perfect. But turf would let hundreds more children play, conserve water, and lower yearly costs. The council should vote yes.

stimuli.title: Passage B: Keep Corbin Park Green
stimuli.html:
Letter to the Editor, by Gary Pruitt, Millbrook resident and volunteer youth soccer coach

[1] I have coached youth soccer at Corbin Park for six years, and I am asking the city council to vote no on the plan to rip out our grass fields and replace them with plastic.

[2] Last spring, my son played an away game on a turf field in another town. He slid for a ball and came home with a burn on his leg the size of my hand. If turf could do that to my son in one game, imagine what it will do to hundreds of kids every week. A coach I know from a neighboring league told me that injuries on his team doubled after his town switched to turf.

[3] Turf also gets dangerously hot. Last July, a local news crew measured the surface of a turf field at Lakeview High School at 152 degrees on a 90-degree afternoon. Grass a few yards away measured 95 degrees. Our kids should not have to play on a surface that hot.

[4] Then there are the health risks. I have read online that turf is full of toxic chemicals, and I would not want my children breathing them in. Why take the chance?

[5] Supporters say turf will save money, but they leave out the replacement costs. Turf wears out, and the city will have to pay millions every few years to replace it. That money could go to our schools instead.

[6] Yes, the grass fields close sometimes after a big rain. But kids have been playing on grass at Corbin Park for seventy years. My grandfather played on this grass, and so should my grandchildren. And make no mistake: once the city puts down plastic fields, the next step will be paving the rest of the park for parking lots.

[7] Corbin Park is the heart of Millbrook. Keep it green.

stimuli.title: A Student's Draft Body Paragraph (contains errors)
stimuli.html: (1) Whitfield’s argument is better supported because she uses city records and addresses the concerns about turf. (2) Whitfield supports her claim with official records. (A), she reports that the two main fields were closed on 46 days last year and that the leagues turned away 210 children. (3) Her figures on water use and maintenance costs (B) also specific and could be checked. (4) Pruitt, on the other hand, relies mostly on stories and fears. (5) His claim about toxic chemicals (C) because he never names a source. (6) Overall, Pruitt’s evidence is weaker (D) Whitfield’s.

stimuli.title: Passage A: Four Days Will Fix What Ails Our Schools
stimuli.html:
By Rick Dorsey, Member, Halden County School Board

[1] Halden County schools are short on money and short on teachers. I have a solution that districts around the country are already using: a four-day school week. Students would attend longer days Monday through Thursday and have Fridays off. I urge the school board to approve this schedule for next fall.

[2] First, a four-day week would save a fortune. A consultant who works for Flexweek, a company that sells four-day scheduling software, estimates that districts like ours can cut costs by up to 20 percent. With one less day of school each week, we would run fewer buses, heat and cool our buildings less, and pay for fewer substitute teachers.

[3] Second, it would solve our teacher shortage. Teachers love the idea of a three-day weekend. My cousin teaches in a four-day district two states away, and she says she will never go back to five days. Once word gets out, teachers will be lining up to work in Halden County.

[4] Third, students would benefit. With Fridays free, they could schedule doctor visits, work part-time jobs, or simply rest. Everybody knows that well-rested students learn more. Some parents worry about finding child care on Fridays, but families have always found a way, and they will again.

[5] Critics warn that test scores could fall. That is nothing but fear of change. If we keep doing things the old way, our district will fall further behind every year until no family wants to live here.

[6] Other districts have been bold. It is time for Halden County to be bold too. Vote yes on the four-day week.

stimuli.title: Passage B: Look Closely Before Canceling Fridays
stimuli.html:
By Dr. Teresa Lindqvist, Professor of Education Policy, Carver State University

[1] I understand why a four-day week appeals to Halden County. Budgets are tight, and teachers are hard to find. But before the school board votes, it should look at what has happened in districts that have already made the change.

[2] The savings are real but small. The state Office of School Finance reviewed the budgets of 120 four-day districts and found that they saved an average of 1.8 percent, mostly on buses and utilities. Salaries, the largest cost in any district, do not shrink, because teachers are paid for the year, not by the day. For Halden County, with a yearly budget of $62 million, a 1.8 percent savings would be about $1.1 million.

[3] The effect on hiring is more promising. In a survey by the same office, 64 percent of teachers in four-day districts said the schedule made them more likely to stay in their jobs. That is a genuine benefit. Still, 4 in 10 of those districts reported unfilled teaching positions three years after switching, so the schedule did not end their shortages.

[4] Learning is the greater concern. My research team compared 40 districts that moved to a four-day week with 40 similar districts that kept five days. After three years, math scores in the four-day districts had grown more slowly, by about the amount students typically learn in two months of school.

[5] Families pay a price, too. When nearby Pine Hollow switched to four days, a district survey found that 38 percent of families with children under 12 had to pay for child care on Fridays, at an average cost of $45 a week.

[6] A four-day week is not a disaster, but it is not a cure. Instead of changing every school next fall, the board should run a two-year pilot at three schools, offer low-cost Friday programs for younger students, and publish the results before making a final decision.

stimuli.title: A Student's Draft Body Paragraph (contains errors)
stimuli.html: (1) Lindqvist's argument is better supported because she relies on state data and admits where the plan could help. (2) (A), she reports that four-day districts saved an average of only 1.8 percent of their budgets, not the 20 percent Dorsey promises. (3) The results of her team's study of 80 districts (B) that math scores grew more slowly under the four-day schedule. (4) Dorsey's evidence, on the other hand, (C). (5) His cousin's experience is one teacher's opinion, and the consultant who gave the 20 percent figure works for a company that sells four-day scheduling software. (6) Dorsey never seriously considers the plan's (D) on learning; he simply calls the concern “fear of change.”

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Whitfield’s main claim in Passage A?
items.hint: Look at the end of paragraph 1 and at paragraph 7, where Whitfield states what she wants the council to do and why.
items.explain:
Step 1: Find where the author states her position. In paragraph 1 she writes, “I urge the council to approve it. Turf would give our young people far more time to play, and it would save water and money.” Paragraph 7 repeats this: “The council should vote yes.”

Step 2: The “convert two Corbin Park fields” choice includes both the position (convert two fields) and her reasons (more playing time, water and money savings).

The “safer than grass in every season” choice is a distortion: Whitfield admits turf gets hotter (paragraph 6) and never says it is safer or that every park should change. Building new fields elsewhere and watering less are never proposed.
options: Millbrook should convert two Corbin Park fields to turf, which would allow more playing time and save water and money.
Millbrook should build new grass fields in another park so that the Corbin Park fields can rest after heavy rain.
Artificial turf is safer than grass in every season, so every park in Millbrook should replace its grass fields with turf.
The city should water the Corbin Park fields less often in summer so that it can save money during dry seasons.
why: Whitfield never proposes building fields somewhere else. Her plan is to convert the existing Corbin Park fields to turf.
This distorts the passage. Whitfield admits turf gets hotter than grass (paragraph 6), and she proposes changing only the two main Corbin Park fields, not every park.
Whitfield mentions water use as a reason for turf, which needs no watering. She never proposes watering the grass less.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Pruitt’s position in Passage B?
items.hint: What does Pruitt ask the council to do in paragraph 1, and what does he say in his last sentence?
items.explain:
Step 1: In paragraph 1 Pruitt says he is “asking the city council to vote no on the plan.” Step 2: In paragraph 7 he ends, “Keep it green.” So his position is to reject the plan and keep grass.

He never asks for more studies, a compromise with one turf field, or shade structures. (Shade structures come from Whitfield’s passage, paragraph 6.) He suggests the money could go to schools, not to shade.
options: The city should spend the turf money on shade structures beside the grass fields.
The city should install turf on one field and keep natural grass on the other one.
The city council should reject the turf plan and keep natural grass at Corbin Park.
The city should delay the turf plan until scientists finish more studies of its safety.
why: Shade structures come from Whitfield's passage (paragraph 6). Pruitt suggests the money could go to schools instead.
Pruitt does not offer a compromise. He wants both fields kept as grass.
Pruitt never asks for more studies. He asks the council to “vote no” and ends with “Keep it green.”

items.prompt: Whitfield claims that grass fields limit how often children can play. Click the sentence from paragraph 2 that provides the most specific evidence for this claim.
items.hint: Specific evidence usually includes a number, a date, or a measurement that could be checked.
items.explain:
Step 1: Look for a sentence with a fact that could be checked. Step 2: Only the 46-day sentence gives a measured fact about the Corbin Park fields: they “were closed on 46 days” last year.

The “serious limit” sentence is a general claim. The sentence about cleats tearing up roots explains why fields close (reasoning) but gives no measurement. The sentence about canceled practices describes effects in general words. The sentence about turf draining quickly is about turf, not about how grass limits play.
spans: Grass fields have served Millbrook well for decades, but they have a serious limit.
When grass is wet, cleats tear up the roots, so the fields must close after heavy rain.
Last year, the two main fields at Corbin Park were closed on 46 days, mostly during the spring and fall league seasons.
Every closure means canceled practices, rescheduled games, and frustrated families.
An artificial turf field drains quickly and can be used again within an hour of a storm.
items.why: Many students click “Every closure means canceled practices, rescheduled games, and frustrated families” because it shows the problem clearly. It describes effects in general words but gives no measurement. The 46-day sentence is the one with a checkable number.

items.prompt: Why is the news crew’s measurement in paragraph 3 of Passage B stronger evidence than the coach’s statement in paragraph 2?
items.hint: Ask two of the evidence questions: Who is the source? Is the evidence specific?
items.explain:
Step 1: The coach is unnamed (“A coach I know”), and his claim that injuries “doubled” is secondhand with no numbers or records. Step 2: The news crew is a more identifiable source (a local news crew measuring at a named school, Lakeview High School), and it reports exact readings: 152 degrees on turf and 95 degrees on grass on a 90-degree afternoon. Step 3: Named, specific, checkable evidence is stronger.

The Corbin Park choice is wrong because the measurement was taken at Lakeview High School, not Corbin Park. Emotional appeal does not make evidence stronger, and length is not a measure of quality.
options: It reports exact readings taken at a named school, which readers could check.
It appeals more strongly to readers' feelings about the safety of young children on hot days.
It uses more words and more detail, and longer pieces of evidence are more convincing to readers.
It is about Corbin Park itself, while the coach's statement is about a team in a different town.
why: Appealing to feelings does not make evidence stronger. The measurement is stronger because of who took it and how specific it is.
Length is not a test of evidence. The coach's statement is weak because it is secondhand and unnamed, not because it is short.
Check the passage: the news crew measured a field at Lakeview High School, not Corbin Park.

items.prompt: Which two statements identify faulty reasoning in Pruitt’s letter? Select two answers.
items.hint: Look for a prediction that jumps from one step to a disaster, and a conclusion based on a single example.
items.explain:
Correct: The parking-lot prediction (paragraph 6) is a slippery slope: Pruitt claims one step will lead to a much worse result but gives no evidence. Using his son’s single burn to predict harm to “hundreds of kids every week” (paragraph 2) is a hasty generalization.

Not faulty: The news crew measurement is specific evidence. Admitting the fields close after rain is a concession, which is fair reasoning. The claim that turf can be hotter is supported by the measurement, and Whitfield agrees with it in paragraph 6.
options: He uses one injury to his son in one game to predict what will happen to hundreds of children every week.
He states that turf can be hotter than grass on summer afternoons.
He predicts that installing turf will lead to paving the rest of the park for parking lots, without evidence that this is planned.
He cites a specific temperature measurement taken by a local news crew.
He admits that the grass fields sometimes close after a big rain.
why: This claim is supported by the news crew's measurement, and Whitfield agrees in paragraph 6. It is not a flaw.
This is specific evidence from an identified source, not faulty reasoning. It is one of Pruitt's stronger points.
Admitting the fields close after rain is a concession, which is fair reasoning. It makes his argument more honest, not less.

items.prompt: How does Whitfield respond to the concern that turf gets hot in summer?
items.hint: Reread paragraph 6. Does she deny the problem or accept it?
items.explain:
Step 1: In paragraph 6, Whitfield writes, “Turf also gets hotter than grass in direct summer sun.” She accepts the concern. Step 2: She lists three steps: light-colored infill, shade structures, and temperature checks, with play pausing at 120 degrees.

She never dismisses the heat, never attacks studies, and never says the fields will close all summer. Acknowledging a problem and offering a solution makes an argument more credible.
options: She argues that the heat is not a real problem because children are used to playing in summer weather.
She says the turf fields will be closed for the entire summer season so that the heat will not matter.
She admits that turf gets hotter than grass and lists steps the city will take to limit the risk.
She claims that the studies showing turf is hotter were paid for by companies that sell grass seed.
why: Whitfield does not dismiss the heat. She writes, “Turf also gets hotter than grass in direct summer sun,” and then offers solutions.
She says play will pause only if the surface reaches 120 degrees. She never says the fields will close for the summer.
Whitfield never mentions who paid for any studies. Attacking a source is not how she handles this concern.

items.prompt: The statements below come from Passage A and Passage B. Drag each statement into the correct category.
items.hint: Ask of each statement: Is there a named source or a number someone could check? Or is it a feeling, a rumor, or a prediction with no proof?
items.explain:
Specific, checkable evidence: The 46 closure days and the $58,000 cost come from the parks department’s own records and include exact figures. The 152-degree and 95-degree readings come from an identified news crew at a named school. Notice that strong evidence can appear in either passage.

Unsupported claim or emotional appeal: “I have read online” names no source and gives no facts. The grandfather sentence appeals to tradition and feelings, not evidence. The paving prediction is a slippery slope with no proof that such a plan exists.
choices: A local news crew measured a turf field at 152 degrees while nearby grass measured 95 degrees. (Passage B)
Last year, the two main fields at Corbin Park were closed on 46 days. (Passage A)
I have read online that turf is full of toxic chemicals. (Passage B)
Once the city puts down plastic fields, the next step will be paving the rest of the park. (Passage B)
Mowing, fertilizing, lining, and reseeding the two fields cost the city $58,000. (Passage A)
My grandfather played on this grass, and so should my grandchildren. (Passage B)
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the 152-degree news crew reading under “Unsupported” because it comes from Pruitt, the weaker passage. Strong evidence can appear in either passage: this reading has an identified source and exact numbers.

items.prompt:
Complete the evaluation of this evidence from Passage B, paragraph 2: “A coach I know from a neighboring league told me that injuries on his team doubled after his town switched to turf.”

The source is {{0}}. The claim {{1}}. As evidence against turf, it is {{2}}.
items.hint: Ask the Source and Specific questions. Who is the coach? Can anyone check the number?
items.explain: Source: the coach is unnamed, and Pruitt is only repeating what he was told, so the evidence is secondhand. Specific: “doubled” sounds precise, but there are no injury counts, dates, or records to check. Verdict: weak. The most tempting wrong choice in the last blank is “strong,” because a doubling sounds alarming; but alarming is not the same as reliable.

options: an unnamed coach, reported secondhand
a measurement taken by a local news crew
an official record from the parks department
a named expert who studied many teams
why: The news crew appears in paragraph 3 and measured temperature, not injuries.
Official records come from Whitfield's department in Passage A. This claim comes from a conversation Pruitt reports.
The coach is never named and is not described as an expert. Pruitt only says he is “a coach I know.”

options: gives no numbers, dates, or records a reader could check
is confirmed by Whitfield in Passage A
cites a published study of turf injuries
includes exact injury counts from a league report
why: Whitfield never mentions injuries. She discusses heat, cost, water, and playing time.
No study is named or cited. The claim rests on what one coach said.
“Doubled” is the only figure, and it comes with no counts, dates, or report. Nothing here can be checked.

options: weak
the strongest evidence in either passage
strong
why: The strongest evidence in the pair comes from named, checkable sources, such as Whitfield's department records or the news crew's readings.
An unnamed, secondhand claim with nothing to check fails the Source and Specific questions, so it cannot be strong.

items.prompt: A student is planning an Extended Response about Passage A and Passage B. Which thesis statement would best begin a high-scoring response?
items.hint: A strong thesis names the better-supported side, gives reasons based on the evidence, and mentions both authors.
items.explain:
Step 1: The thesis must answer the prompt: which position is better supported. Step 2: It should give reasons drawn from the evidence. Step 3: It should refer to both passages.

The “city records” thesis does all three. The “I have played on it” choice is personal opinion and uses no evidence from the passages. The “both make good points” choice takes no position. The “cares more” choice picks a side but supports it with an assumption about who “cares more,” which is not evidence and is not stated in either passage.
options: Pruitt's argument is better supported because he is a volunteer coach who works with children every week and clearly cares more about them than Whitfield does.
Whitfield's argument is better supported because she uses city records on closures, costs, and water and answers the heat concern, while Pruitt relies on one story and fears.
Both Whitfield and Pruitt make good points about Corbin Park, and the city council will face a hard decision when it finally votes on the turf plan.
I think artificial turf is better than grass because I have played on it many times myself and it never gets muddy or torn up after a big storm.
why: This picks a side, but its reason is an assumption about who “cares more,” which is not evidence and is not stated in either passage.
This takes no position. Fairness belongs in the body of the essay, but the thesis must choose a side.
This is personal opinion based on the writer's own experience. It never mentions either passage or says which author is better supported.

items.prompt:
Read the student’s draft paragraph. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these sentences.

Sentence 2: Whitfield supports her claim with official records. {{0}}, she reports that the two main fields were closed on 46 days last year and that the leagues turned away 210 children.

Sentence 3: Her figures on water use and maintenance costs {{1}} also specific and could be checked.

Sentence 5: His claim about toxic chemicals {{2}} because he never names a source.

Sentence 6: Overall, Pruitt’s evidence is weaker {{3}} Whitfield’s.
items.hint: (A) Does the sentence give an example or a contrast? (B) Find the subject: is it singular or plural? (C) Which choice sounds formal? (D) Which word is used for comparisons?
items.explain:
Blank (A): Sentence 2 states that Whitfield uses official records; the next part gives instances of those records. A transition that introduces an example is needed: For example. “However” and “In contrast” signal an opposite idea, and “Otherwise” signals an alternative, so they do not fit.

Blank (B): The subject is “figures” (not “costs,” which is part of the phrase “on water use and maintenance costs”). “Figures” is plural, and the paragraph is in present tense, so the verb is are. “Is,” “was,” and “has been” are singular.

Blank (C): An essay needs a formal, precise tone (part of Trait 2). is less convincing is formal. “Kinda sketchy” and “no good at all” are informal, and “totally fails” is an exaggeration in casual language.

Blank (D): Use than to compare (“weaker than”). “Then” refers to time. “That” and “as” do not complete a comparison with “weaker.”

options: For example
Otherwise
In contrast
However
why: “Otherwise” signals an alternative or a consequence. Nothing here is an alternative; it is an example.
“In contrast” signals an opposite idea. The sentence continues the same idea with an example.
“However” signals a contrast, but the sentence gives an example of the official records named in sentence 2.

options: has been
was
is
are
why: “Has been” is singular. The plural subject “figures” needs a plural verb.
“Was” is singular and past tense. The subject “figures” is plural, and the paragraph is in present tense.
“Is” is singular. The subject is “figures,” which is plural; “costs” is inside the phrase “on water use and maintenance costs.”

options: is kinda sketchy
is no good at all
totally fails
is less convincing
why: “Kinda sketchy” is slang. An essay needs a formal tone, which is part of Trait 2.
“Is no good at all” is informal and vague. It does not say how the claim falls short.
“Totally fails” is casual and exaggerated. A formal, precise phrase is better.

options: than
as
that
then
why: “As” is used in “as weak as.” After “weaker,” the comparison needs “than.”
“That” does not complete a comparison. “Weaker that Whitfield's” is not standard English.
“Then” is about time (first this, then that). Comparisons use “than.”

items.prompt:
A student is writing a thesis for an Extended Response about Passage A and Passage B. Choose the options that make the strongest thesis.

{{0}}'s argument is better supported because she {{1}}, while {{2}} relies mostly on {{3}}.
items.hint: Name the side whose evidence passes the five questions, and describe each author's evidence accurately.
items.explain: A strong thesis names the better-supported side, gives evidence-based reasons, and mentions both authors. Whitfield is better supported: she uses department records on closures, water, and costs and admits turf's drawbacks, while Pruitt relies mostly on one personal story, an unnamed source, and fears about the future (his son's burn, the coach he knows, the online claim, and the paving prediction). The most tempting wrong choice is “proves that turf is safer,” which sounds strong but overstates what Whitfield says.

options: Pruitt
The city council
Whitfield
why: Pruitt's letter rests mostly on one story, an unnamed coach, an online rumor, and a slippery slope. His side is the weaker one.
The city council did not write either passage. The thesis must name one of the two authors.

options: proves that turf is safer than grass in every season
has worked for the city longer than Pruitt has coached
uses department records on closures, water, and costs and admits turf's drawbacks
shares a moving story about children who were turned away
why: This distorts the passage. Whitfield admits turf gets hotter than grass in summer; she never claims it is safer in every season.
Neither passage says how long Whitfield has worked for the city. Even if it did, years on the job are not evidence about turf.
Whitfield reports a number (210 children turned away), not a moving story. Praising her for emotion misses why her evidence is strong.

options: the news crew
Whitfield
Pruitt
why: The news crew is a source Pruitt cites, not an author. Its reading is actually one of Pruitt's stronger pieces of evidence.
Whitfield is already the subject of the sentence. The “while” part must name the other author.

options: data on how many children were turned away
one personal story, an unnamed source, and fears about the future
official measurements and a careful look at both sides
a clear plan to replace the turf every ten years
why: The 210 children turned away is Whitfield's evidence, from her paragraph 3.
This describes a strong argument. Pruitt mostly relies on his son's burn, “a coach I know,” “I have read online,” and a slippery slope.
The ten-year replacement plan is in Whitfield's passage, not Pruitt's.

items.prompt: A student argues that Whitfield’s position is better supported. Which detail from Pruitt’s letter could the student most effectively show to be inaccurate by using information from Whitfield’s passage?
items.hint: Find a statement by Pruitt about something Whitfield discusses directly with specific facts. Then check whether her facts contradict him.
items.explain:
Step 1: In paragraph 5, Pruitt says supporters “leave out the replacement costs” and that the city will pay “millions every few years.” Step 2: In her paragraph 5, Whitfield does discuss replacement: the surface lasts “about ten years” and costs “about $450,000 per field.” For two fields, that is 2 × $450,000 = $900,000 about every ten years, not millions every few years. Step 3: So Whitfield’s facts directly contradict both parts of Pruitt’s claim.

The 152-degree choice misreads Whitfield: 120 degrees is the temperature at which play will pause, not a limit on how hot turf can get. She agrees turf gets hot. Pruitt’s coaching experience and his description of the park are not contradicted by anything in Passage A.
options: Pruitt's statement that he has coached youth soccer at Corbin Park for six years, since Whitfield says that the leagues turned away 210 children this fall
Pruitt's report that a news crew measured a turf field at 152 degrees on a July afternoon, since Whitfield says that turf never gets hotter than 120 degrees
Pruitt's claim that the city will pay “millions every few years” to replace turf, since Whitfield gives the replacement cost and says the surface lasts about ten years
Pruitt's description of Corbin Park as “the heart of Millbrook,” since Whitfield says that the park's two main fields were closed on 46 days last year
why: Nothing in Whitfield's passage contradicts Pruitt's coaching experience. The 210 children is about field space, not about Pruitt.
This misreads Whitfield. 120 degrees is the temperature at which play will pause, not a limit on how hot turf gets. She agrees turf gets hot.
A field closing on some days does not contradict calling the park the heart of the town. That phrase is an opinion, not a fact Whitfield disputes.

items.prompt:
Read this paragraph from a student’s Extended Response about the turf passages.

Artificial turf is the right choice for Millbrook. When I was in high school, our team played on turf, and we never had to cancel a game because of mud. Furthermore, turf looks bright and clean all year, while grass turns brown in August. In addition, young people today need more places to exercise, and turf fields can be used in almost any weather. For these reasons, the city should install turf as soon as possible.

Which rubric trait does this paragraph most need to improve, and why?
items.hint: Check what the paragraph uses as evidence. Does it mention Whitfield, Pruitt, or anything from their passages?
items.explain:
Step 1: Check Trait 3. The sentences are clear and correctly written, so Trait 3 is not the main problem. Step 2: Check Trait 2. The paragraph uses transitions (“Furthermore,” “In addition,” “For these reasons”) and has a clear order. Step 3: Check Trait 1. The paragraph never mentions either author or any evidence from the passages. It argues what the writer thinks the city should do, supported by the writer’s own high school experience. The task is to decide which passage is better supported, using evidence from both.

So Trait 1 needs the most improvement. A clear position with reasons is not enough when the reasons do not come from the texts.
options: Trait 1, because it argues the writer's own opinion from personal experience instead of judging the two passages
None of the traits, because it states a clear position on turf and gives three separate reasons to support that position
Trait 2, because it has no transitions to connect its ideas and no clear order from its first sentence to its last
Trait 3, because it contains many errors in grammar, spelling, and punctuation that make its sentences hard to follow
why: A clear position with reasons is not enough when the reasons come from the writer's life instead of the passages. The task is to judge which passage is better supported.
The paragraph does use transitions (“Furthermore,” “In addition,” “For these reasons”) and follows a clear order.
Reread the paragraph: its sentences are clear and correctly written. Trait 3 is not the main problem.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, Whitfield admits that “Our yearly savings would cover about half of that future cost, not all of it.” How does this admission most likely affect her argument?
items.hint: Think about how readers react when an author admits a drawback openly instead of hiding it. Is cost part of her claim?
items.explain:
Step 1: Check the math she is describing. Savings: about $46,000 a year × 10 years = about $460,000. Replacement: 2 fields × $450,000 = $900,000. $460,000 is about half of $900,000, so her statement is accurate.

Step 2: Consider the effect. By stating a drawback openly with figures, Whitfield shows she is not hiding information, which makes her other numbers more trustworthy. Her main reasons (more playing time and lower yearly costs) still stand.

The “destroys her argument” choice overstates the effect: she never claimed turf would fully pay for itself. She does not agree the city cannot afford turf; she still urges a yes vote. Cost is related to her claim, because saving money is one of her main reasons.
options: It strengthens her credibility, because she openly states a limitation with numbers, which makes her other figures more believable.
It destroys her argument, because she admits that the turf fields will not completely pay for themselves over time.
It shows that she secretly agrees with Pruitt that the city cannot afford to install and replace the turf fields.
It has no effect on her argument, because the cost of the turf fields is not related to the claim she makes.
why: This overstates the effect. Whitfield never claimed turf would fully pay for itself, and her main reasons (playing time and lower yearly costs) still stand.
She still urges a yes vote in paragraph 7. Admitting a cost is not the same as agreeing the city cannot afford turf.
Saving money is one of her main reasons, so cost is directly related to her claim.

items.prompt: A student has decided that Whitfield's argument is better supported. Which plan for the body paragraphs would best organize the response?
items.hint: The plan should match the thesis, use both passages, and judge the evidence rather than summarize it.
items.explain: The plan must match the thesis (Whitfield is better supported) and use both passages. The correct plan gives one paragraph to the weaknesses of Pruitt's evidence (his son's single burn, the online claim), one to the strengths of Whitfield's records (46 closure days, 1,100 vs. 3,000 hours, 1.3 million gallons), and one to fairness: Pruitt's best point, the 152-degree reading, and Whitfield's answer (light infill, shade, temperature checks). The summary plan is the most tempting because it uses both passages, but summarizing is not evaluating.
options: Body 1: Pruitt's points about heat and injuries; Body 2: his point about tradition and his grandfather; Body 3: why the city should keep Corbin Park green
Body 1: a summary of Whitfield's passage; Body 2: a summary of Pruitt's letter; Body 3: the student's own experience of playing on turf fields in high school
Body 1, Body 2, and Body 3: Whitfield's figures on closures, playing hours, and water, leaving out Pruitt's letter because it is the weaker of the two passages
Body 1: flaws in Pruitt's evidence, such as the single burn and the online claim; Body 2: Whitfield's records; Body 3: Pruitt's heat point and her answer
why: This plan argues for Pruitt's side, which does not match the student's thesis that Whitfield is better supported.
Summaries retell the passages without judging them, and personal experience is not evidence from the texts. This plan would score low on Trait 1.
The prompt requires evidence from both passages. Pruitt's weak evidence is half of the proof that Whitfield is better supported.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Dorsey's main claim in Passage A?
items.hint: Look at the end of paragraph 1 and at paragraph 6, where Dorsey tells the board what to do.
items.explain: Step 1: Find the claim. Paragraph 1 ends: “I urge the school board to approve this schedule for next fall,” and paragraph 6 repeats, “Vote yes on the four-day week.” Step 2: His main reasons are money (paragraph 2) and teachers (paragraph 3). The correct choice gives both the position and the reasons. The child care choice is tempting because child care comes up, but Dorsey dismisses the issue rather than proposing a solution.
options: Halden County should hire a consultant from Flexweek to study whether a four-day week would suit its schools.
Halden County should keep five school days but make each one shorter so that students can get more rest.
Halden County should switch its schools to a four-day week next fall to save money and attract teachers.
Halden County should offer free child care on Fridays so that parents can support a four-day school week.
why: Dorsey cites a Flexweek consultant as evidence; he never asks the board to hire one for a study.
Dorsey wants longer days Monday through Thursday and no school on Friday, not five shorter days.
Dorsey mentions child care only to wave off parents' worries (“families have always found a way”). He never proposes free child care.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Lindqvist's position in Passage B?
items.hint: Reread paragraph 6. Does she say “never,” “now,” or something in between?
items.explain: Paragraph 6 states her position: “Instead of changing every school next fall, the board should run a two-year pilot at three schools… and publish the results before making a final decision.” The “reject for good” choice is the most tempting because she raises concerns, but she explicitly says the plan “is not a disaster.”
options: The board should adopt the four-day week next fall, because it helps districts keep their teachers.
The board should not switch every school next fall but should test the schedule in a pilot first.
The board should cut teacher salaries, since salaries are the largest cost in any school district.
The board should reject the four-day week for good, because it has failed in every district that tried it.
why: She admits the hiring benefit in paragraph 3, but her conclusion is to test the schedule first, not to adopt it everywhere next fall.
She mentions salaries to explain why savings are small. She never proposes cutting them.
This overstates her view. She writes that a four-day week “is not a disaster” and suggests a pilot, not a permanent ban.

items.prompt: Lindqvist claims that the savings from a four-day week are small. Click the sentence from paragraph 2 that reports measured findings from a named source.
items.hint: Look for a sentence that says who measured something and what they found.
items.explain: The second sentence names its source (the state Office of School Finance), tells how much was studied (120 districts' budgets), and reports a measured result (1.8 percent average savings). The first sentence is the claim itself. The salaries sentence is reasoning that explains why savings are small. The $1.1 million sentence applies the 1.8 percent to Halden's budget ($62 million × 0.018 ≈ $1.1 million); it is a useful calculation, but it is not the research finding.
spans: The savings are real but small.
The state Office of School Finance reviewed the budgets of 120 four-day districts and found that they saved an average of 1.8 percent, mostly on buses and utilities.
Salaries, the largest cost in any district, do not shrink, because teachers are paid for the year, not by the day.
For Halden County, with a yearly budget of $62 million, a 1.8 percent savings would be about $1.1 million.
items.why: Many students click the $1.1 million sentence because it has the biggest number. That sentence applies the finding to Halden County; the measured finding itself, with its named source, is the state review of 120 districts.

items.prompt: Why is the state Office of School Finance review in Passage B stronger evidence than the consultant's estimate in Passage A?
items.hint: Ask two of the evidence questions: Who is the source, and what do they gain? What exactly was measured?
items.explain: Step 1: The consultant works for Flexweek, “a company that sells four-day scheduling software,” so the source gains if districts switch. “Up to 20 percent” is a best case, not an average. Step 2: The state office has nothing to sell and reviewed 120 real budgets, reporting an average of 1.8 percent. Step 3: An independent, specific, measured source beats a biased estimate. The Halden County choice is tempting, but the review studied other districts; Lindqvist only applies its average to Halden.
options: It reports a larger savings figure, and larger savings make a stronger case for the four-day week.
It is about Halden County's own budget, while the consultant's estimate is about other districts.
It comes from a public agency with nothing to sell and reports an average from 120 actual budgets.
It appeals more to readers' feelings about tight budgets and about the teachers who are hard to find.
why: Check the numbers: the review found 1.8 percent, much smaller than the consultant's “up to 20 percent.” The review is stronger because of its source and method, not its size.
The review studied 120 other four-day districts, not Halden County. Lindqvist only applies its average to Halden's budget.
Strong evidence persuades with facts, not feelings. The review is stronger because of who did it and what it measured.

items.prompt: Which two statements identify faulty reasoning in Dorsey's passage? Select two answers.
items.hint: Look for a prediction that jumps to disaster and a conclusion drawn from one person's experience.
items.explain:
Correct: The prediction that the district will fall behind “until no family wants to live here” (paragraph 5) is a slippery slope: an extreme chain of events with no evidence. Using one cousin's experience to predict that teachers “will be lining up” (paragraph 3) is a hasty generalization.

Not faulty: fewer buses and lower utility costs is reasonable, and Passage B confirms savings come from those areas. Describing the plan and stating the claim are not reasoning errors.
options: He uses his cousin's experience in one district to predict that teachers will line up to work in Halden County.
He describes the plan as longer school days Monday through Thursday with no classes on Fridays.
He predicts that keeping five days will make the district fall behind until no family wants to live there, without evidence.
He asks the school board to approve the four-day schedule so that it can begin next fall.
He explains that one less school day would mean fewer bus runs and lower heating and cooling costs.
why: This simply describes the plan. A description is not an argument, so it cannot be faulty reasoning.
This is Dorsey's claim, what he wants the board to do. A claim is not a flaw in reasoning.
This is sound reasoning, and Lindqvist agrees: the savings come “mostly on buses and utilities.” His mistake is the size of the savings, not this logic.

items.prompt: How does Lindqvist respond to the idea that a four-day week helps districts keep teachers?
items.hint: Reread paragraph 3. Does she deny the benefit, accept it, or something in between?
items.explain: In paragraph 3, Lindqvist accepts the point: 64 percent of teachers said the schedule made them more likely to stay, and “That is a genuine benefit.” Then she adds a limit: “4 in 10 of those districts reported unfilled teaching positions three years after switching.” Granting a point and then showing its limits with data is a fair way to handle the other side. The software-company choice mixes up the passages.
options: She grants that the survey shows a real benefit, then notes that many districts still had unfilled jobs.
She claims the teacher survey was paid for by a company that sells four-day scheduling software.
She says teacher hiring does not matter, because salaries are already the largest cost in a district.
She rejects the idea, arguing that teachers dislike longer school days and will quit in large numbers.
why: That describes Dorsey's consultant, who works for Flexweek. The teacher survey came from the state Office of School Finance.
Salaries come up in paragraph 2 to explain why savings are small. She never says hiring does not matter.
Lindqvist does not reject the idea. She calls the hiring effect “more promising” and “a genuine benefit.”

items.prompt: The statements below come from Passage A and Passage B. Drag each statement into the correct category.
items.hint: Ask of each statement: Is there a named source or a number someone could check? Or is it a feeling, a sweeping claim, or a prediction with no proof?
items.explain:
Specific, checkable evidence: the 1.8 percent review and the 64 percent survey come from a named state office and give exact figures; the Pine Hollow figure comes from a district survey with an exact percentage.

Unsupported claim or emotional appeal: “Teachers love the idea” is a sweeping claim with no source. “Everybody knows” is a bandwagon appeal. “Until no family wants to live here” is a slippery slope with no proof.
choices: 64 percent of teachers in four-day districts said the schedule made them more likely to stay. (Passage B)
In Pine Hollow, 38 percent of families with children under 12 paid for Friday child care. (Passage B)
Teachers love the idea of a three-day weekend. (Passage A)
Everybody knows that well-rested students learn more. (Passage A)
The state Office of School Finance found that 120 four-day districts saved an average of 1.8 percent. (Passage B)
Our district will fall further behind every year until no family wants to live here. (Passage A)
items.why: The most common mistake is putting “Teachers love the idea of a three-day weekend” under evidence because Passage B's survey seems to agree. As Dorsey writes it, the sentence has no source and no numbers; it is a sweeping claim about all teachers.

items.prompt:
Complete the evaluation of this evidence from Passage A, paragraph 2: “A consultant who works for Flexweek, a company that sells four-day scheduling software, estimates that districts like ours can cut costs by up to 20 percent.”

The source {{0}}. The figure “up to 20 percent” {{1}}. Compared with the state review in Passage B, this evidence is {{2}}.
items.hint: Ask: who is the consultant working for, and what does “up to” mean?
items.explain: Source: the consultant works for Flexweek, which sells four-day scheduling software, so the source profits if districts switch. Specific: “up to 20 percent” is the top of a range, a best case, not a measured average. Verdict: weaker than the state review, which found an average of 1.8 percent across 120 real budgets. The tempting wrong answer in the second blank mixes up the two passages' numbers.

options: is a research team that compared 80 districts
is a teacher who works in a four-day district
is an independent agency with nothing to gain
works for a company that profits if districts switch
why: That is Lindqvist's research team in Passage B. The 20 percent figure comes from a Flexweek consultant.
That is Dorsey's cousin in paragraph 3, not the source of the 20 percent figure.
That describes the state Office of School Finance in Passage B. This consultant works for a company that sells four-day scheduling software.

options: is the average savings found in 120 real budgets
is a best-case estimate, not an average of actual savings
is the amount Halden County saved during a pilot
is confirmed by Lindqvist's research team
why: The average from 120 real budgets is Passage B's 1.8 percent. “Up to” means the most a district might save.
Halden County has not run a pilot. Lindqvist recommends one in paragraph 6.
Lindqvist's figures contradict it: the average savings were 1.8 percent, not 20 percent.

options: stronger
weaker
equally strong
why: A best-case estimate from a source that profits is weaker than an average from 120 real budgets reported by an independent agency.
The two are not equal: one source has something to sell and gives a best case, while the other measured real results.

items.prompt: A student is planning an Extended Response about Passage A and Passage B. Which thesis statement would best begin a high-scoring response?
items.hint: A strong thesis names the better-supported side, gives reasons based on the evidence, and mentions both authors.
items.explain: A strong thesis names the better-supported side, gives evidence-based reasons, and mentions both authors. The correct thesis does all three: Lindqvist (side), state data and a study of 80 districts (reasons), and “while Dorsey relies on…” (both authors). The school-board choice is the most tempting because it picks a side with a reason, but the reason is a job title, not evidence.
options: Lindqvist's argument is better supported because she relies on state data and a study of 80 districts, while Dorsey relies on a seller's estimate and a relative's story.
Dorsey's argument is better supported because he serves on the school board himself and understands the needs of Halden County better than a professor ever could.
Dorsey and Lindqvist both make strong points about the four-day week, and the Halden County school board will have a very difficult choice to make this year.
I think a four-day school week is a great idea, because I would love to have every Friday off to rest, catch up on errands, and spend more time with my family.
why: This picks a side because of Dorsey's job, not his evidence. Being on the board does not make a seller's estimate or a cousin's story reliable.
This takes no position. The thesis must name the better-supported side; fairness can come later in the essay.
This is personal opinion about Fridays off. It never says which author is better supported or uses either passage.

items.prompt:
Read the student's draft paragraph. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these sentences.

Sentence 2: {{0}}, she reports that four-day districts saved an average of only 1.8 percent of their budgets, not the 20 percent Dorsey promises.

Sentence 3: The results of her team's study of 80 districts {{1}} that math scores grew more slowly under the four-day schedule.

Sentence 4: Dorsey's evidence, on the other hand, {{2}}.

Sentence 6: Dorsey never seriously considers the plan's {{3}} on learning; he simply calls the concern “fear of change.”
items.hint: (A) Example or contrast? (B) Find the subject: singular or plural? (C) Which sounds formal? (D) Noun or verb?
items.explain:
Blank (A): Sentence 1 says Lindqvist relies on state data; sentence 2 gives an instance of it, so the transition is For example.

Blank (B): The subject is “results” (plural), not “study.” A plural subject in present tense takes show.

Blank (C): The essay needs a formal judgment: is much less convincing. The other choices are slang or insulting.

Blank (D): After the possessive “the plan's,” a noun is needed. Effect is the noun meaning “result”; “affect” is usually the verb.

options: For example
However
In contrast
Otherwise
why: “However” signals a contrast, but sentence 2 gives an example of the state data named in sentence 1.
“In contrast” signals an opposite idea. Sentence 2 continues the same idea with an example.
“Otherwise” signals an alternative or a consequence. Sentence 2 is an example, not an alternative.

options: shows
was showing
show
has shown
why: “Shows” is singular. The subject is “results,” which is plural; “study” is inside the phrase “of her team's study.”
“Was showing” is singular and past tense. The plural subject “results” needs “show,” and the paragraph is in present tense.
“Has shown” is singular. The plural subject “results” would need “have shown.”

options: is much less convincing
is super shaky
is a total joke
kind of falls apart

“A total joke” is insulting and informal. It mocks instead of evaluating.
“Kind of falls apart” is casual and vague. A formal phrase states the judgment clearly.

options: effected
effect
affect
affects

“Affect” is usually a verb (to influence). After “the plan's,” the sentence needs a noun, a result: “effect.”
“Affects” is a verb. The blank follows the possessive “the plan's,” so it needs a noun.

items.prompt:
A student is writing a thesis for an Extended Response about Passage A and Passage B. Choose the options that make the strongest thesis.

{{0}}'s argument is better supported because she {{1}}, while {{2}} relies mostly on {{3}}.
items.hint: Name the side whose evidence passes the five questions, and describe each author's evidence accurately.
items.explain: Lindqvist is better supported: she uses state budget data and a study of 80 districts and admits where the plan helps, while Dorsey relies mostly on a seller's estimate, one relative's story, and warnings with no proof (the Flexweek consultant, his cousin, “everybody knows,” and the slippery slope in paragraph 5). The tempting “has a doctorate” choice names the right author but gives a credential instead of evidence.

options: Flexweek
Lindqvist
Dorsey
why: Flexweek is a company mentioned in Passage A, not an author. The thesis must name one of the two authors.
Dorsey's evidence is a seller's estimate, a cousin's story, and predictions with no proof. His side is the weaker one.

options: has a doctorate and teaches at a large state university
proves that the four-day week has failed everywhere
uses state budget data and a study of 80 districts and admits where the plan helps
describes the stress parents feel about Friday child care
why: A title is not evidence. Her argument is strong because of what her data show, not because of her degree.
This distorts the passage. She says the four-day week “is not a disaster” and admits a hiring benefit.
Lindqvist reports a survey figure (38 percent paid for child care), not parents' feelings. Calling it an emotional appeal misses why it is strong.

options: Dorsey
Lindqvist
the state Office of School Finance

options: a review of 120 district budgets
a careful pilot program with published results
a seller's estimate, one relative's story, and warnings with no proof
teacher survey data gathered by the state

The pilot program is Lindqvist's recommendation in paragraph 6. Dorsey wants to switch every school next fall.
The state teacher survey appears in Lindqvist's paragraph 3, not in Dorsey's passage.

items.prompt: A student argues that Lindqvist's position is better supported. Which claim from Dorsey's passage could the student most effectively show to be inaccurate by using information from Lindqvist's passage?
items.hint: Find a claim by Dorsey that Lindqvist discusses with specific facts. Then check whether her facts contradict it.
items.explain: Step 1: Dorsey says the change “would save a fortune” and cites “up to 20 percent.” Step 2: Lindqvist reports that 120 four-day districts saved an average of 1.8 percent, because salaries, the largest cost, “do not shrink.” For Halden's $62 million budget, 1.8 percent is about $1.1 million (62,000,000 × 0.018 = 1,116,000), while 20 percent would be $12.4 million. Step 3: Her data directly contradict his claim. The teacher choice is tempting, but her survey supports the idea that teachers like the schedule; what her data challenge is his claim that it would solve the shortage.
options: Dorsey's statement that teachers like the idea of a three-day weekend, since Lindqvist reports that 64 percent of teachers were more likely to stay
Dorsey's description of longer school days Monday through Thursday, since Lindqvist says the board should run a two-year pilot at three schools
Dorsey's claim that students could use Fridays for doctor visits, since Lindqvist reports that many Pine Hollow families paid for Friday child care
Dorsey's claim that the change would “save a fortune,” since Lindqvist reports average savings of 1.8 percent because salaries do not shrink
why: Lindqvist's survey actually supports this idea rather than contradicting it. Use evidence that shows the claim is inaccurate.
Lindqvist does not dispute how the schedule works. Recommending a pilot is about timing, not about the length of school days.
Paying for child care does not contradict students using Fridays for appointments. Both can be true, so this does not show Dorsey is wrong.

items.prompt:
Read this paragraph from a student's Extended Response about the four-day week passages.

Lindqvist argument is more better then Dorseys because she use real numbers. like the state found districts only save 1.8 percent its not alot. Dorsey just say his cousin like it which dont prove nothing about other teachers.

Which rubric trait does this paragraph most need to improve, and why?
items.hint: First check whether the paragraph uses the passages. Then read each sentence for grammar and punctuation.
items.explain: Step 1: Check Trait 1. The paragraph takes a position (Lindqvist is better supported), uses evidence from both passages, and even explains why the cousin's story is weak. Step 2: Check Trait 3. It has many errors: “Lindqvist argument” (missing ’s), “more better then” (double comparison and then/than), “she use” (agreement), a fragment starting with “like,” “its” for “it's,” “alot,” “Dorsey just say,” and the double negative “dont prove nothing.” These errors make the sentences hard to read, so Trait 3 needs the most work. The “None” choice is tempting because the reasoning is good, but the errors interfere with clarity.
options: Trait 1, because it never uses evidence from either passage and never names either of the two authors
Trait 2, because it argues the writer's own personal opinion about whether four-day weeks are a good idea
Trait 3, because errors in grammar, punctuation, and word choice make the sentences hard to read
None of the traits, because it takes a clear position and supports it with evidence from both passages
why: Reread the paragraph: it names both authors and uses evidence from each (the 1.8 percent figure, the cousin). Its ideas are sound; its sentences are not.
The paragraph does not argue a personal opinion. It judges the authors' evidence, which is what the task asks.
The ideas are on target, but errors such as “more better then,” “she use,” a fragment beginning with “like,” and “dont prove nothing” would cost points.

items.prompt: In paragraph 3, Lindqvist writes, “That is a genuine benefit.” How does this statement most likely affect her argument?
items.hint: Think about how readers react when an author admits a point for the other side and then tests it with data.
items.explain: By admitting that the hiring effect is “a genuine benefit,” Lindqvist shows she is weighing the evidence honestly instead of hiding what does not help her. She then limits the point with data: 4 in 10 districts still had unfilled jobs. Fair handling of the other side makes her other figures more believable. The “agrees with Dorsey” choice is tempting, but she agrees only that there is a benefit, not that it solves the shortage.
options: It makes her more credible, because she admits a point in the plan's favor and then shows its limits with data.
It weakens her argument, because it shows that she secretly favors switching every school to four days next fall.
It has no effect on her argument, because teacher hiring has nothing to do with her position on the school plan.
It shows that she agrees with Dorsey that a four-day week would solve the district's teacher shortage for good.
why: Her conclusion still recommends a pilot instead of switching every school. Admitting one benefit is not the same as changing sides.
Hiring is one of Dorsey's two main reasons, so how she handles it matters directly to the debate.
She says the opposite: 4 in 10 districts still had unfilled positions, so “the schedule did not end their shortages.”

items.prompt: A student has decided that Lindqvist's argument is better supported. Which plan for the body paragraphs would best organize the response?
items.hint: The plan should match the thesis, use both passages, and judge the evidence rather than summarize it.
items.explain: The plan must match the thesis (Lindqvist is better supported) and use both passages. The correct plan gives one paragraph to the weaknesses of Dorsey's evidence (the Flexweek consultant, his cousin), one to the strengths of Lindqvist's evidence (1.8 percent across 120 budgets, the 80-district comparison), and one to fairness: Dorsey's best point, hiring, and how Lindqvist answers it with the survey and the 4-in-10 figure. The summary plan is tempting because it uses both passages, but summarizing is not evaluating.
options: Body 1: flaws in Dorsey's evidence, such as the seller's estimate and the cousin; Body 2: Lindqvist's state data and study; Body 3: Dorsey's hiring point and her answer
Body 1: a summary of Dorsey's passage; Body 2: a summary of Lindqvist's passage; Body 3: the student's own memories of how tired students were on Fridays
Body 1: Dorsey's points about savings and buses; Body 2: his point about well-rested students; Body 3: why Halden County should be bold and vote yes next fall
Body 1, Body 2, and Body 3: Lindqvist's figures on savings, hiring, and math scores, leaving out Dorsey's passage because it is the weaker of the two passages
why: Summaries retell the passages without judging them, and memories are not evidence from the texts. This plan would score low on Trait 1.
This plan argues for Dorsey's side, which does not match the student's thesis that Lindqvist is better supported.
The prompt requires evidence from both passages. Dorsey's weak evidence is half of the proof that Lindqvist is better supported.

stimuli.title: Paired Passages: Library Fines
stimuli.html:
Passage A: End Overdue Fines at the Marlowe City Library

By Angela Ruiz, Director, Marlowe City Public Library

[1] Every year, our library blocks thousands of residents from borrowing because they owe overdue fines. Last year, 4,300 card holders, about one in nine, could not check out materials because they owed more than $10. The city council should end overdue fines.

[2] Fines do not bring in much money. Last year they brought in $38,000, less than 1 percent of the library's budget, and staff spent about 600 hours collecting them.

[3] Fines also do not seem to get books back faster. During a six-month trial without fines at our two largest branches, 94 percent of items came back within two weeks of the due date, compared with 93 percent at the same branches the year before.

[4] Some residents worry that people will keep books forever. Under our plan, any item more than 30 days overdue would be billed as lost, and borrowing would pause until the item is returned or paid for.

Passage B: Fines Teach Responsibility

By Dale Harmon, Member, Marlowe City Council

[1] Ending library fines sends exactly the wrong message. When I was a boy, I paid my overdue fines out of my allowance, and it taught me to be responsible. Kids today need that same lesson.

[2] Everyone I know who uses the library thinks the fines are fair. And the director's trial lasted only six months at two branches, hardly enough time to prove anything.

[3] The $38,000 that fines bring in is real money. If we give it up, what comes next? Soon the library will stop charging for lost books too, and our shelves will be empty.

stimuli.title: Paired Passages: Downtown Parking Meters
stimuli.html:
Passage A: Free Parking Will Save Main Street

By Lou Brennan, Owner, Brennan's Hardware

[1] Shoppers are tired of feeding parking meters, and Main Street is paying the price. The city should remove the meters downtown and offer free two-hour parking instead.

[2] Three stores on my block closed last year. Customers tell me all the time that they would rather drive to the mall, where parking is free.

[3] A friend who owns a bakery in Dunmore says business boomed after that town removed its meters. If it worked in Dunmore, it will work here.

[4] The meters bring in nothing but pocket change for the city. If we keep them, soon every store downtown will be empty.

Passage B: Meters Keep Spaces Open for Customers

By Priya Natarajan, Transportation Planner, City of Ashby

[1] Removing the meters sounds friendly to shoppers, but city data show it would make parking harder to find downtown. The council should keep the meters.

[2] In a city count last spring, 88 percent of downtown spaces were full at noon on weekdays. Studies of other downtowns have found that when parking is free, employees often take the best spaces for the whole day, leaving fewer open for customers.

[3] The meters brought in $410,000 last year. That money pays for downtown sidewalk repair and the free weekend shuttle.

[4] Store owners are right that some shoppers find the meters frustrating. That is why the city plans to add pay-by-phone and make the first 15 minutes free.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Ruiz's claim and her main reasons?
items.explain: Ruiz states her claim at the end of paragraph 1: “The city council should end overdue fines.” Her reasons follow: fines block 4,300 card holders (paragraph 1), bring in only $38,000, less than 1 percent of the budget (paragraph 2), and do not speed returns (94 percent vs. 93 percent, paragraph 3). The lost-books choice is tempting because lost items come up, but Ruiz's plan keeps charging for them.
options: The city should extend the no-fine trial to every branch for another year before it makes any final decision.
The city should end overdue fines, because they block many borrowers, raise little money, and do not speed returns.
The library should stop charging for lost books, because many borrowers simply forget to return their items.
The city should raise overdue fines, because $38,000 a year is too little to cover the cost of collecting them.
why: Ruiz asks the council to end fines now. Questioning the length of the trial is Harmon's point, not a proposal from Ruiz.
This reverses her plan. Under her plan, items more than 30 days overdue would be billed as lost.
Ruiz uses the $38,000 figure to show fines are not worth keeping. She never proposes raising them.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from Ruiz's passage that provides the strongest evidence that fines do not get books back faster.
items.explain: The claim is about return speed, so the evidence must measure returns. Only the trial sentence does: 94 percent of items came back within two weeks without fines, compared with 93 percent with fines at the same branches. Removing fines did not slow returns. The $38,000 sentence is about money, the blocked-borrowers sentence is about access, and the 30-day sentence describes the plan.
spans: Every year, our library blocks thousands of residents from borrowing because they owe overdue fines.
Last year they brought in $38,000, less than 1 percent of the library's budget, and staff spent about 600 hours collecting them.
During a six-month trial without fines at our two largest branches, 94 percent of items came back within two weeks of the due date, compared with 93 percent at the same branches the year before.
Under our plan, any item more than 30 days overdue would be billed as lost, and borrowing would pause until the item is returned or paid for.
items.why: Some students click the $38,000 sentence because it has specific numbers. It is strong evidence that fines raise little money, but it says nothing about how quickly books come back.

items.prompt: Which point in Harmon's passage is the most reasonable?
items.explain: A fair reader admits when the weaker side makes a good point. Harmon's question about the trial is reasonable: six months at two branches is a limited sample, and a strong essay could acknowledge it. His other points fail the five questions: the allowance story is one case (Sufficient), “everyone I know” is a bandwagon appeal (Source), and the empty-shelves prediction is a slippery slope that Ruiz's 30-day rule answers.
options: Ending fines will lead the library to stop charging for lost books, and then the shelves will be empty.
Everyone he knows who uses the library thinks that the library's overdue fines are completely fair.
Paying his own fines as a boy taught him responsibility, so all of today's children need fines too.
The trial lasted only six months at two branches, which is a limited test of a citywide change.
why: This is a slippery slope, and Ruiz's plan contradicts it: items more than 30 days overdue would still be billed as lost.
This is a bandwagon appeal from an unnamed group. What his friends think does not prove fines work.
This is a hasty generalization: one man's childhood experience is turned into a rule for all children.

items.prompt: Which two statements identify faulty reasoning in Harmon's passage? Select two answers.
items.explain: Bandwagon: “Everyone I know who uses the library thinks the fines are fair” uses popularity among an unnamed group as proof. Slippery slope: “Soon the library will stop charging for lost books too, and our shelves will be empty” predicts a chain of events with no evidence, and Ruiz's plan to bill long-overdue items as lost contradicts it. Questioning the trial's length is the most reasonable point in his passage, so it is not faulty.
options: He states his position that ending library fines sends the wrong message.
He notes that the fines brought in $38,000, the same figure that Ruiz reports.
He treats the fact that everyone he knows thinks the fines are fair as proof that fines should stay.
He predicts that ending fines will lead to free lost books and empty shelves, without any evidence.
He questions whether a six-month trial at two branches is long enough to prove anything.
why: This is Harmon's claim. Stating a position is not a reasoning error.
Citing an accurate figure is not a flaw. Both authors agree on the $38,000; they disagree about whether it matters.
This is a reasonable question about the evidence, not faulty reasoning. A limited trial is a fair concern.

items.skill: Deciding which side is better supported
items.prompt: Which argument is better supported, and why?
items.explain: Ruiz's evidence passes the five questions: it comes from library records (Source), uses exact figures (Specific), measures the outcomes she claims (Relevant), and she answers the main worry about books never coming back (Fair). Harmon relies on an anecdote, a bandwagon appeal, and a slippery slope. The “longer passage” choice is the most tempting because it names Ruiz, but a GED response must give evidence-based reasons, not length.
options: Harmon's, because he points out that the $38,000 the fines bring in is real money the library would lose.
Ruiz's, because her figures come from library records and she answers the worry that books will not come back.
Harmon's, because he is an elected council member who speaks for the residents who use the library.
Ruiz's, because her passage is longer than Harmon's passage and includes many more numbers than his does.
why: Harmon uses Ruiz's own figure, but he never answers her point that it is less than 1 percent of the budget and takes about 600 staff hours to collect.
An elected title is not evidence. Harmon's claims rest on a childhood story, a bandwagon appeal, and a slippery slope.
This names the right side for the wrong reason. Length and the number of figures do not decide support; reliable sources and fair handling of the other side do.

items.prompt:
Choose the options that make the strongest thesis for a response to these passages.

The tempting “proves that no borrower will ever keep a library book” overstates what Ruiz says.

Ruiz
The city council

proves that no borrower will ever keep a library book
describes how unfair fines feel to struggling families
has run the library longer than Harmon has served on the council

options: Ruiz
Harmon
the library staff

options: the library's records on blocked card holders
a plan to bill long-overdue items as lost
return rates measured during a six-month trial
a childhood story, a bandwagon appeal, and a slippery slope

items.prompt:
Read this body paragraph from a student's response to the library passages.

Ruiz is the director of the library. She says that 4,300 card holders were blocked last year and that fines brought in $38,000. She also describes a six-month trial at two branches. Harmon is a member of the city council. He says he paid fines as a boy and that everyone he knows thinks the fines are fair. He also worries that the shelves will be empty.

It reports what each author says, accurately and in order, but it never makes a judgment: it does not say Ruiz's records are reliable, that Harmon's “everyone I know” is a bandwagon appeal, or which side is better supported. Evaluating evidence is the core of Trait 1. The “None” choice is the most tempting because the paragraph uses details from both passages, but details without judgment earn little.
options: Trait 2, because it jumps between the two passages in a random order with no logical plan at all
None of the traits, because it uses specific details from both passages, which is what the task asks
Trait 1, because it retells both passages but never judges whose evidence is stronger or explains why

items.prompt: A student's thesis says Ruiz's argument is better supported. Drag each planning note into the body paragraph where it belongs.
items.explain: Body 1 tests the weaker side: the bandwagon appeal and the slippery slope. Body 2 shows the stronger side's evidence: the return rates and the small fine revenue. Body 3 treats the other side fairly: the worry about books never coming back and how Ruiz's plan answers it.
choices: Fines brought in $38,000, less than 1 percent of the library's budget.
“Everyone I know who uses the library thinks the fines are fair” is a bandwagon appeal.
The worry that people will keep books forever, and Ruiz's plan to bill items over 30 days late as lost.
