items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Natarajan's claim and her main reasons?
items.explain: Natarajan's claim is in paragraph 1: “The council should keep the meters.” Her reasons: spaces are already scarce (88 percent full at noon, paragraph 2), and meter money pays for sidewalk repair and the weekend shuttle (paragraph 3). The remove-the-meters choice is tempting because she agrees shoppers find meters frustrating, but that is a concession, not her position.
options: The city should build a new parking garage, because 88 percent of downtown spaces are full at noon on weekdays.
The city should keep the meters, because spaces are already scarce and meter money pays for downtown needs.
The city should remove the meters, because shoppers find them frustrating and stores downtown are closing.
The city should charge downtown employees for all-day parking, because they take the best spaces from shoppers.
why: Natarajan uses the 88 percent figure to show parking is scarce. She never proposes a garage.
This is Brennan's position. Natarajan admits some shoppers find meters frustrating, but she argues to keep them.
She mentions employees taking spaces to explain what happens when parking is free. She does not propose a new charge for employees.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from Natarajan's passage that gives the most specific, checkable evidence that downtown parking is already hard to find.
items.explain: The city count is a measurement of Ashby's own downtown with a specific result: 88 percent of spaces full at noon on weekdays. It could be checked. The first sentence states the claim. The studies sentence supports what free parking would do, but the studies are unnamed. The $410,000 sentence is about money, not parking supply.
spans: Removing the meters sounds friendly to shoppers, but city data show it would make parking harder to find downtown.
In a city count last spring, 88 percent of downtown spaces were full at noon on weekdays.
Studies of other downtowns have found that when parking is free, employees often take the best spaces for the whole day, leaving fewer open for customers.
The meters brought in $410,000 last year.
items.why: Some students click the “studies of other downtowns” sentence because it mentions research. Those studies are not named, and they describe other places; the city count is a named, specific measurement of this downtown.

items.prompt: Which point in Brennan's passage is the most reasonable?
items.explain: A fair reader admits when the weaker side has a point. Brennan says shoppers are tired of feeding meters, and Natarajan herself agrees: “Store owners are right that some shoppers find the meters frustrating.” His other points fail the five questions: the Dunmore story is one secondhand case (Sufficient), “pocket change” is contradicted by $410,000 (Specific), and “every store downtown will be empty” is a slippery slope.
options: The parking meters bring in nothing but pocket change for the city.
If the city keeps the meters, soon every store downtown will be empty.
If removing meters worked in Dunmore, it will work in Ashby too.
Shoppers are tired of feeding the parking meters downtown.
why: Natarajan reports that the meters brought in $410,000 last year, which is not pocket change. This claim is unsupported and contradicted.
This is a slippery slope: a prediction of total collapse with no evidence.
This is a hasty generalization: one friend's report about one bakery in one town becomes a rule for Ashby.

items.prompt: Which two statements identify faulty reasoning in Brennan's passage? Select two answers.
items.explain: Hasty generalization: “If it worked in Dunmore, it will work here” turns one friend's report about one bakery into a rule. Slippery slope: “soon every store downtown will be empty” predicts collapse with no evidence. Stating his claim, describing the plan, and noting that mall parking is free are not reasoning errors.
options: He predicts that keeping the meters will leave every store downtown empty, without evidence.
He notes that parking at the mall is free, unlike parking downtown.
He explains that the free parking he wants would be limited to two hours.
He uses one friend's report about a bakery in Dunmore to predict what will happen in Ashby.
He states what he wants: removing the meters and offering free two-hour parking.
why: This is an accurate fact about the mall. Stating it is not faulty reasoning.
This describes his proposal. A description is not a flaw in reasoning.
This is Brennan's claim. Stating a position is not a reasoning error.

items.skill: Deciding which side is better supported
items.prompt: Which argument is better supported, and why?
items.explain: Natarajan's evidence passes the five questions: a city count of 88 percent full (Source, Specific), $410,000 in meter money with named uses (Specific, Relevant), and a fair answer to shoppers' frustration with pay-by-phone and 15 free minutes (Fair). Brennan relies on a friend's story, unexplained store closings, and a slippery slope. The “longer passage” choice is the most tempting because it names Natarajan, but the reason is length, not evidence.
options: Natarajan's, because her figures come from city counts and budgets and she answers shoppers' complaints.
Natarajan's, because her passage is longer than Brennan's passage and includes many more numbers than his.
Brennan's, because he reports that three stores on his block closed last year after shoppers went elsewhere.
Brennan's, because he runs a store downtown and hears directly from his customers about the meters.

vocab.def: The 45-minute typed essay on the GED RLA test in which you analyze two opposing arguments and explain which one is better supported.
vocab.example: For the Extended Response, I read two articles about a ballpark and wrote about which was better supported.

vocab.def: A piece of writing that tries to convince readers to accept a position by giving reasons and evidence.
vocab.example: Osei's argument is that taxpayers should not pay for the ballpark.

vocab.def: The main position an author wants readers to accept.
vocab.example: Bell's claim: the city should pay $48 million for a ballpark.

vocab.def: Facts, numbers, research, examples, or expert statements that an author uses to prove a claim.
vocab.example: Repaying $3.1 million a year for 25 years is evidence about cost.

vocab.def: The explanation that connects evidence to a claim and shows why the evidence proves it.
vocab.example: Fans mostly live in town, so their spending moves around instead of growing.

vocab.def: Backed by evidence that is more reliable, specific, relevant, and sufficient than the other side's evidence.
vocab.example: Osei's position is better supported because her evidence is independent and specific.

vocab.def: How believable and trustworthy a source or author is.
vocab.example: An independent economist has more credibility on stadium costs than a study paid for by the team.

vocab.def: A slant toward one side, often because the source gains something from a particular result.
vocab.example: A study paid for by the team that wants the ballpark may be biased.

vocab.def: A short personal story used as evidence; it can make a point vivid but cannot prove a pattern by itself.
vocab.example: Bell's story about his brother-in-law in Harlan City is an anecdote.

vocab.def: Faulty reasoning that draws a broad conclusion from too few examples.
vocab.example: "It worked in one city, so it will work everywhere."

vocab.def: Faulty reasoning that says something must be right because many people support it.
vocab.example: "Everyone I talk to downtown is excited."

vocab.def: A point that goes against an author's position; strong writers acknowledge it and respond to it.
vocab.example: Osei admits losing the team would disappoint fans, then offers another plan.

vocab.def: One sentence, usually at the end of the introduction, that states which argument is better supported and why.
vocab.example: Osei's argument is better supported because she relies on independent research and specific cost figures.

vocab.def: One of the three qualities the GED essay rubric scores, each from 0 to 2 points.
vocab.example: Trait 1 is creation of arguments and use of evidence.

vocab.def: A pattern for body paragraphs: Point (a judgment), Evidence (a quote or paraphrase), Explain (why the evidence is strong or weak), Link (back to the thesis or the other passage).
vocab.example: Point: Bell's evidence is weaker than it looks. Evidence: the 1,200 jobs come from a team-paid study. Explain: the team gains from the result. Link: Osei, by contrast, cites independent research.

notes:
Week 9 RLA Study Sheet: The Extended Response I

The task

  • 45 minutes, typed, two opposing passages
  • Decide which position is better supported (not which you agree with)
  • Use specific evidence from both passages

The rubric (each trait 0–2)

  1. Arguments and evidence: clear position; specific, relevant evidence from both texts; explain why it is strong or weak
  2. Development and organization: intro, body, conclusion; logical order; transitions; precise word choice; formal style and tone
  3. Clarity and standard English conventions: clear, varied sentence structure; no run-ons or fragments; correct grammar and punctuation

Trait total 0–6, doubled: up to 12 RLA raw points.

Five evidence questions

  1. Source: who, expert, independent?
  2. Specific: numbers, dates, named studies?
  3. Relevant: proves this claim?
  4. Sufficient: enough, or one story?
  5. Fair: deals with the other side?

Red flags

  • Hasty generalization: one case → rule
  • Bandwagon: “everyone agrees”
  • Slippery slope: one step → disaster
  • Emotional appeal in place of proof
  • Unnamed source: “I read online”
  • Source that profits from the result

Thesis: three jobs

Name the side · give evidence-based reasons · mention both authors. Put it at the end of the introduction.

___’s argument is better supported because ___, while ___ relies on ___.

P-E-E-L body paragraph

Point → Evidence (quote or paraphrase) → Explain (why strong or weak) → Link (back to thesis or other passage)

Essay plan and timing

StepJob
Plan (~10 min)Read, highlight, organizer, thesis
IntroductionIssue, both authors’ positions, thesis
Body 1Weaknesses of the weaker passage
Body 2Strengths of the stronger passage
Body 3 (optional)Best point of the weaker side and how the stronger side answers it
ConclusionRestate thesis in new words (writing total ~28 min)
Check (~7 min)Both passages used? Errors fixed?

Specific is not the same as reliable. Always ask who produced the evidence and what they gain.

Judgment words to use: strong, weak, reliable, biased, specific, vague, unsupported, credible, relies on, fails to.
